questions.stem:
With reference to Mughal India, what is/are the difference/differences between Jagirdar and Zamindar?
1. Jagirdars were holders of land assignments in lieu of judicial and police duties, whereas Zamindars were holders of revenue rights without obligation to perform any duty other than revenue collection.
2. Land assignments to Jagirdars were hereditary and revenue rights of Zamindars were not hereditary.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements invert the actual position.**

**Statement 1 — wrong.** A *jagir* was an assignment of the land revenue of an area to a **mansabdar in lieu of cash salary** for military and administrative service — not for judicial and police duties. And zamindars were far from duty-free: they maintained local law and order, kept armed retainers, and supplied troops when called; revenue collection (for which they kept the *nankar*, roughly 10%) was only one function.

**Statement 2 — wrong, and reversed.** Jagirs were **transferable and non-hereditary** — the state shuffled jagirdars every 3–4 years precisely to stop them striking roots (the shortage of good jagirs, the *be-jagiri* crisis, is a standard Aurangzeb-era answer). Zamindari right, by contrast, was **hereditary and saleable** — a proprietary right in the soil that passed to heirs.

So neither statement is a correct difference → **(d)**.

questions.stem: With reference to land reforms in independent India, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The ceiling laws were aimed at family holdings and not individual holdings.
The major aim of land reforms was providing agricultural land to all the landless.
It resulted in cultivation of cash crops as a predominant form of cultivation.
Land reforms permitted no exemptions to the ceiling limits.
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (b)**

This is an elimination question, and three of the four options contain a hard factual error. (b) contains only a rhetorical stretch. That is the whole decision.

### Why (b) stands

Land reform in independent India had four components: **abolition of intermediaries** (zamindari, jagirdari, inamdari), **tenancy reform** (security of tenure, rent regulation, conferment of ownership on tenants), **ceilings on holdings with redistribution of the surplus**, and **consolidation of fragmented holdings**. The declared objective running through all of them, from the First Plan onwards, was **"land to the tiller"** — end absentee ownership and put the soil in the hands of the person who actually works it. The ceiling chapter states this most directly: surplus land declared above the ceiling was to be distributed to **landless agricultural labourers and marginal farmers**, with priority to SC/ST allottees.

So (b) restates the textbook *aim*. Note what the option does **not** say: it does not say land reform *succeeded* in giving land to all the landless. It plainly did not — only about 2% of the net sown area was ever declared surplus, roughly 5 million acres were distributed, and the great bulk of the landless got nothing. But the option is a statement of purpose, and the record of failure is an answer to a different question.

### Why (a) fails — the exclusion, not the noun

(a) is where a well-prepared solver goes, because "family holding" is a real term of art in ceiling law and it is genuinely the unit most textbooks emphasise. The error is not in the words *family holdings*. It is in **"and not individual holdings."**

The history has two phases and (a) describes only the second:

- **First phase, c. 1958–1972.** Every state had ceiling legislation on the books by the early 1960s, and in most of them the **unit of application was the individual**, not the family. This is precisely why the first round failed so completely. If the ceiling attaches to a person, a landholder simply partitions the estate on paper among wife, adult sons, minor children and fictitious transferees — the *benami* transfers that swallowed the surplus before it could be declared.
- **Second phase, from 1972.** The **National Guidelines of 1972**, adopted after the Chief Ministers' Conference, changed the unit of application from the individual to the **family** (taken as five members) and lowered the ceilings sharply: about 10 acres of best irrigated two-crop land, 15 acres of land with assured irrigation for one crop, 27 acres of dry land, with additional land for families above five members subject to an outer limit of twice the ceiling.

Even after 1972 the exclusion in (a) is not clean: individuals outside a family unit remained subject to ceilings in their own right, and several state Acts counted **adult/major sons as separate units**, which reopened the same partition loophole. So "family holdings and **not** individual holdings" is wrong for the entire first phase and imprecise for the second.

Rewrite (a) as *"after 1972 the unit of application for the ceiling shifted from the individual to the family"* and it becomes correct — and UPSC would have had to write it that way. As printed, it is an exclusionary claim about the design of ceiling law, and the exclusion is false.

### Why (d) fails — and what it teaches about (b)

(d) is the other absolute in the set, and here the absolute **is** fatal, because it is a claim about what the statutes actually said. Exemptions from the ceiling were extensive and are the standard critique of the whole exercise: **plantations of tea, coffee, rubber and cardamom; orchards; specialised livestock, dairy and seed farms; sugarcane farms held by cooperatives and factories; and land held by religious, charitable and educational trusts.** These carve-outs, together with the individual-unit loophole, are why so little land was ever declared surplus.

The contrast with (b) is the point of the question. Both options carry a universal quantifier. In (d) the quantifier governs **what the law provided**, and it is contradicted by the text of the Acts. In (b) the quantifier governs **what the policy was trying to achieve** — and an objective can be framed universally even when performance falls far short. A solver who rejects (b) for the word "all" has to apply the same reasoning to (d) and reject that too, at which point every option is gone.

### Why (c) fails

Cash crops never became the predominant form of cultivation. **Foodgrains have continuously occupied roughly two-thirds of the gross cropped area** since Independence. And the cropping-pattern change that did occur — the shift to HYV wheat and rice — was the **Green Revolution**, which was a *foodgrain* intensification, driven by seed-fertiliser-irrigation technology and price support, not by land reform. Land reform's measurable effect on the crop mix was close to nil.

### The takeaway

When one option states an **aim** and another states a **rule**, read the quantifier differently in each. "All" inside a purpose is aspiration; "no exemptions" inside a statute is a testable claim, and one counterexample kills it. And treat every exclusion — *X and not Y* — as two claims: (a) here is true about the family unit and false about the individual unit, and half-true is wrong.
questions.tagging_note: Gap in the syllabus tree: no topic covers post-independence land reforms (zamindari abolition, tenancy reform, land ceiling laws) directly. ECO-14 (agriculture policy) is the nearest GS fit and GEO-17 touches the agrarian-structure side. SOC-23 does name land reforms explicitly, but Sociology is the optional subject with pyq_drills = false, so it should not receive a GS1 PYQ.
questions.review_flag: Official key says b, worked solution said a (medium confidence).

questions.stem: The Global Competitiveness Report is published by the
options: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
questions.explanation_md:
**Global Competitiveness Report → World Economic Forum (WEF), Geneva** — published annually since 1979.

Keep the publisher list straight:
- **WEF:** Global Competitiveness Report, Global Risks Report, Global Gender Gap Report, Travel & Tourism Competitiveness, Energy Transition Index.
- **World Bank:** Ease of Doing Business, World Development Report, Global Economic Prospects, Human Capital Index.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about 'the Charter Act of 1813' :
1. It ended the trade monopoly of the East India Company in India except for trade in tea and trade with China.
2. It asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Indian territories held by the Company.
3. The revenues of India were now controlled by the British Parliament.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Charter Act of 1813 — statements 1 and 2 correct, 3 wrong.**

**1 — correct.** It **ended the Company's trade monopoly in India**, throwing Indian trade open to all British merchants, but the Company **retained its monopoly of the tea trade and of trade with China** (both went only in 1833).

**2 — correct.** This is the Act that for the first time **expressly asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown** over the Company's Indian territories.

**3 — wrong.** Indian revenues stayed under the **Company's** administration; the Act only required it to keep **separate commercial and territorial accounts** and sanctioned Rs 1 lakh a year for education. Parliamentary/Crown control over Indian revenue and administration came in stages later — 1833 (Company becomes purely administrative) and finally **1858**, when the Crown took over.

Also remember 1813: **Christian missionaries were allowed in** (the "pious clause") and the Company's charter was renewed for 20 years.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles HIS and POL: the Charter Acts sit in Spectrum's constitutional-development chapter (HIS-03) and are also revised as Laxmikanth Ch.1 historical background (POL-01). Tagged HIS as primary since the framing is the 1813 Act's trade and revenue provisions, not constitutional evolution.

questions.stem:
With reference to Swadeshi Movement, consider the following statements :
1. It contributed to the revival of the indigenous artisan crafts and industries.
2. The National Council of Education was established as a part of Swadeshi Movement.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are correct.**

**1 — correct.** The economic core of Swadeshi (1905–08) was **boycott of foreign goods plus positive promotion of indigenous production**: swadeshi textile mills, soap and match factories, tanneries, banks and insurance, national handloom and artisan crafts, and enterprises like **Bengal Chemicals (P. C. Ray)**. Whatever its long-run commercial fate, it did give a real fillip to indigenous crafts and industry.

**2 — correct and it is the deciding fact.** The **National Council of Education was set up on 15 August 1906** to organise education "on national lines and under national control"; the **Bengal National College** opened with **Aurobindo Ghosh as its principal**, and the Bengal Technical Institute (later Jadavpur University) grew out of the same impulse.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Movement/Organization* | *Leader* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. All India Anti-Untouchability League | Mahatma Gandhi |
| 2. All India Kisan Sabha | Swami Sahajanand Saraswati |
| 3. Self-Respect Movement | E. V. Ramaswami Naicker |

Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
**All three pairs are correctly matched.**

1. **All India Anti-Untouchability League — Gandhi.** Founded **September 1932, immediately after the Poona Pact**, with **G. D. Birla as president and Amritlal Thakkar as secretary**; renamed the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** in 1933, with the weekly *Harijan* as its voice. ✔
2. **All India Kisan Sabha — Swami Sahajanand Saraswati.** Founded at **Lucknow, April 1936**, with Sahajanand as **first president** and **N. G. Ranga as general secretary**. ✔
3. **Self-Respect Movement — E. V. Ramaswami Naicker (Periyar)**, launched in **1925** in Tamil Nadu against Brahminical dominance and caste ritual; it pioneered self-respect marriages without priests. ✔
questions.tagging_note: Each pair lands in a different topic: Kisan Sabha in HIS-15 (peasant movements), Self-Respect Movement in HIS-05 (socio-religious reform), and the All India Anti-Untouchability League in HIS-12 (post-Poona Pact anti-untouchability work). HIS-15 chosen as primary because it is the broadest social-movements bucket. Format is 'pairs' rather than match_list — three numbered pairs asking which are correctly matched, not a List I / List II grid.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is **not** a Harappan site?
questions.explanation_md:
**Sohgaura is not Harappan — it is Mauryan.**

**Sohgaura (Gorakhpur district, UP)** is famous for the **Sohgaura copper-plate inscription**, a Mauryan-era record in Brahmi about **famine relief and storehouses** — nothing to do with the Indus civilisation.

The other three are all Harappan:
- **Chanhudaro** — Sindh, on the Indus; the only Harappan city **with no citadel**, a bead- and bangle-making centre.
- **Kot Diji** — Sindh, opposite Mohenjodaro; a **pre-Harappan/Early Harappan** culture site that continues into the mature phase.
- **Desalpur** — **Kutch, Gujarat**; a fortified Harappan settlement.

questions.stem: In which of the following relief sculpture inscriptions is 'Ranyo Ashoka' (King Ashoka) mentioned along with the stone portrait of Ashoka?
questions.explanation_md:
**Kanganahalli** (Sannati, **Gulbarga district, Karnataka**, on the Bhima river).

Excavations at this Buddhist *mahastupa* yielded a relief panel showing a king under an umbrella with attendants, labelled in Brahmi **"Rāya Asoko" / "Ranyo Ashoka"** — the **only known sculpted portrait of Ashoka with an inscription naming him**. The site's drum slabs also carry Satavahana-period Jataka and life-of-Buddha reliefs.

Rule out the rest: **Sanchi** has Ashokan pillar and later gateways but no labelled portrait; **Shahbazgarhi** (Pakistan) has a **Rock Edict in Kharoshthi**, not sculpture; **Sohgaura** has a Mauryan **copper-plate**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles ANM and ART: the Ranyo Ashoka inscription is Mauryan epigraphy (ANM-05) but the medium is a stupa relief panel at Kanganahalli, which falls under ART-01 (stupas and early Buddhist architecture). Tagged ANM primary because the testable fact is the Ashokan inscription and portrait.

questions.stem:
Consider the following :
1. Deification of the Buddha
2. Treading the path of Bodhisattvas
3. Image worship and rituals
Which of the above is/are the feature/features of Mahayana Buddhism?
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are Mahayana features.**

1. **Deification of the Buddha** — he ceases to be only a teacher and becomes a transcendent, worshipped being (trikaya doctrine); the historical Buddha is one manifestation. ✔
2. **Path of the Bodhisattva** — the defining Mahayana ideal: postponing one's own nirvana to liberate all beings (Avalokiteshvara, Manjushri, Maitreya), against the Hinayana *arhat* ideal of individual liberation. ✔
3. **Image worship and rituals** — Mahayana gave Buddhism its **anthropomorphic images** (Mathura and Gandhara schools), bhakti-style devotion, offerings and ritual; earlier Buddhism used only symbols — stupa, bodhi tree, wheel, footprints. ✔

Also associated: Sanskrit instead of Pali, and the **Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka** as its formal turning point.

questions.stem: With reference to forced labour (Vishti) in India during the Gupta period, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: It was considered a source of income for the State, a sort of tax paid by the people.
It was totally absent in the Madhya Pradesh and Kathiawar regions of the Gupta Empire.
The forced labourer was entitled to weekly wages.
The eldest son of the labourer was sent as the forced labourer.
questions.explanation_md:
**Vishti was effectively a tax paid in labour** — an unpaid obligation the state could demand from villagers, listed in Gupta-period land grant inscriptions **alongside other fiscal levies such as bhaga, bhoga and hiranya**, and often transferred to the grantee along with the land. That is exactly why it counts as "a source of income for the State, a sort of tax paid by the people".

Why the others fail:
- **(b)** Vishti is attested precisely in **central India (Madhya Pradesh) and Kathiawar/Saurashtra** inscriptions — the region where it is best documented, not absent.
- **(c)** It was **forced and unremunerated**; there were no weekly wages.
- **(d)** No rule made the **eldest son** the designated labourer; the obligation fell on villagers/peasants generally, by turn.

questions.stem: Building 'Kalyaana Mandapas' was a notable feature in the temple construction in the kingdom of
questions.explanation_md:
**Kalyana Mandapa — the pillared "marriage hall" — is the signature addition of Vijayanagara temple architecture.**

The Vijayanagara style (Hampi, Vellore, Kanchipuram, Tadpatri, 14th–16th c.) added three things to the older Dravida temple:
- **Kalyana mandapa** — hall for the annual ceremonial marriage of the deity and consort
- **Amman shrine** — a separate shrine for the consort goddess
- **Composite/monolithic piers** — a central shaft ringed by rearing *yali* (hippogryph) brackets

Quick elimination: **Chalukya** = Vesara experiments at Aihole/Badami/Pattadakal; **Chandela** = Khajuraho, Nagara with *panchayatana* and sculptural bands; **Rashtrakuta** = rock-cut Kailasa at Ellora. None of them built kalyana mandapas.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. In the revenue administration of Delhi Sultanate, the in-charge of revenue collection was known as 'Amil'.
2. The Iqta system of Sultans of Delhi was an ancient indigenous institution.
3. The office of 'Mir Bakshi' came into existence during the reign of Khalji Sultans of Delhi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — correct.** In Sultanate revenue administration the *amil* was the officer who actually collected land revenue at the local level, under the *diwan-i-wizarat*. (*Mushrif* kept accounts, *khut/muqaddam* were village intermediaries.)

**Statement 2 — wrong. The iqta was an imported West Asian institution, not an ancient indigenous one.** It came from the Islamic world (Buwayhid Iran, developed under the Seljuqs) and was brought to India by Iltutmish, who systematised it. It was an assignment of revenue in lieu of salary — non-hereditary and transferable, exactly to prevent it hardening into a landed nobility.

**Statement 3 — wrong.** *Mir Bakshi* is a **Mughal** office (head of the military/mansabdari department, paymaster, from Akbar's reign). The Sultanate's military head was the *ariz-i-mamalik*, made famous under Alauddin Khalji.

Only 1 is correct → **(a)**.
questions.tagging_note: Statements 1 and 2 are pure Delhi Sultanate revenue/iqta administration (ANM-11); statement 3 turns on Mir Bakshi being a Mughal office, hence ANM-14 as a genuine second tag.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Saint Nimbarka was a contemporary of Akbar.
2. Saint Kabir was greatly influenced by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — wrong.** Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita / *bhedabheda*, Radha-Krishna worship, Nimbarka Sampradaya) belongs to roughly the **12th–13th century** — centuries before **Akbar (1556–1605)**. The Vaishnava acharyas placed near Akbar's era are people like Vallabhacharya and Chaitanya (both c. 1479–1533), not Nimbarka.

**Statement 2 — wrong, and impossible on dates. Kabir died c. 1518; Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi was born in 1564.** A man cannot be influenced by someone born forty-odd years after his death. Kabir's guru was traditionally **Ramananda**. Sirhindi (*Mujaddid Alf-i Sani*) went the opposite way ideologically — he attacked Akbar's liberalism and Ibn Arabi's *wahdat-ul-wujud*, offering *wahdat-ul-shuhud* instead.

Neither is correct → **(d)**.

questions.stem:
With reference to the British colonial rule in India, consider the following statements :
1. Mahatma Gandhi was instrumental in the abolition of the system of 'indentured labour'.
2. In Lord Chelmsford's 'War Conference', Mahatma Gandhi did not support the resolution on recruiting Indians for World War.
3. Consequent upon the breaking of Salt Law by Indian people, the Indian National Congress was declared illegal by the colonial rulers.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — correct.** Gandhi's campaign (with Madan Mohan Malaviya and C.F. Andrews) forced the government to end recruitment of **indentured labour in 1917**, the system he had fought in South Africa.

**Statement 2 — wrong, and it is the trap. At Lord Chelmsford's War Conference (Delhi, April 1918) Gandhi *did* support the recruitment resolution** — he spoke one sentence in Hindustani backing it, and then went campaigning for recruits in Kheda, which cost him much popularity. He justified it as earning claim to swaraj through partnership in the Empire's danger.

**Statement 3 — correct.** After the Dandi march and the mass breaking of the salt law, the government **declared the Congress illegal (1930)** and jailed Gandhi, Nehru and the working committee.

1 and 3 → **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Statements 1 and 2 (indentured labour, Chelmsford War Conference 1918) sit in HIS-10; statement 3 (Salt Law breach, INC declared illegal) is Civil Disobedience, HIS-11.

questions.stem:
With reference to Indian National Movement, consider the following pairs :

| *Person* | *Position held* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru | President, All India Liberal Federation |
| 2. K. C. Neogy | Member, The Constituent Assembly |
| 3. P. C. Joshi | General Secretary, Communist Party of India |

Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
**All three pairs are correctly matched.**

1. **Tej Bahadur Sapru** — a leading Moderate who left Congress after 1920; **President of the All India Liberal Federation** (the Moderates' body founded 1918 as the National Liberal Federation). Also known for the Sapru Committee (1945) and the Round Table Conferences.
2. **K. C. Neogy** — **member of the Constituent Assembly**, minister in the interim/first cabinet, and the **first Chairman of the Finance Commission (1951)**.
3. **P. C. Joshi** — **General Secretary of the CPI**, 1935–1947, the party's first and youngest general secretary.

Nothing to eliminate → **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects. Best home is HIS-16 (personalities of the national movement), but P.C. Joshi as CPI General Secretary belongs to the labour/left movements strand (HIS-15) and K.C. Neogy's Constituent Assembly membership is Polity (POL-02). Format: not literally a 'how many pairs' question, but it is pair-matching with three numbered pairs, so 'pairs' fits better than stmt_1_2_3 or match_list (no List I/List II).

questions.stem: With reference to Mian Tansen, which one of the following statements is **not** correct?
options: Tansen was the title given to him by Emperor Akbar.
Tansen composed Dhrupads on Hindu gods and goddesses.
Tansen composed songs on his patrons.
questions.explanation_md:
Asked for the statement that is **NOT** correct.

**(a) is the false one: Akbar gave him the title "Mian", not "Tansen".** Born **Ramtanu Pandey**, he was given the title **"Tansen" by Raja Vikramajit (Man Singh's line) of Gwalior**, whose court he served, before Raja Ramchandra of Rewa sent him to Akbar in 1562. At Akbar's court he became one of the *navaratna* and was honoured as **Mian Tansen**.

The other three are true: he composed **dhrupads on Hindu deities** (Shiva, Krishna) even while a Mughal courtier; he composed **songs praising his patrons** (including Akbar); and he is credited with **new ragas — Miyan ki Malhar, Miyan ki Todi, Darbari Kanada.**

questions.stem: Who among the following Mughal Emperors shifted emphasis from illustrated manuscripts to album and individual portrait?
questions.explanation_md:
**Jahangir** shifted Mughal painting from illustrated manuscripts to the **muraqqa (album) and the individual portrait**.

- **Akbar** = narrative manuscript painting on a workshop scale — *Hamzanama*, *Akbarnama*, *Razmnama*; many hands on one page.
- **Jahangir**, a connoisseur who claimed he could name the artist of any face, wanted **single-artist studies**: portraits, **allegorical/durbar paintings** (Jahangir preferring a Sufi shaikh to kings), **birds and animals from life** (Mansur's Siberian crane, zebra, turkey-cock), and **jharokha portraits**. Star artists: **Abul Hasan** (*Nadir-uz-Zaman*), **Ustad Mansur** (*Nadir-ul-Asr*), Bishandas, Govardhan.
- Under **Shah Jahan** the style hardened into formal, jewel-like court portraiture.

questions.stem: Which one of the following National Parks lies *completely* in the temperate alpine zone?
questions.explanation_md:
**Valley of Flowers (Uttarakhand) lies entirely above ~3,200 m — the whole park is alpine, so it alone is *completely* in the temperate-alpine zone.** It is a UNESCO World Heritage site along with adjoining Nanda Devi NP, and holds alpine meadows, Brahma Kamal, blue poppy, snow leopard and Asiatic black bear.

The others all begin in the tropical/subtropical lowlands, so they cannot be *completely* alpine:
- **Manas** (Assam) — Terai floodplain, near sea level, tropical.
- **Namdapha** (Arunachal) — the widest altitude range of any Indian park, roughly **200 m to 4,500 m**, tropical evergreen through to alpine; famous for four big cats.
- **Neora Valley** (West Bengal, Kalimpong) — about **180 m to 3,200 m**, subtropical to temperate; red panda habitat.

The key word in the stem is **completely**.
questions.tagging_note: Tests national-park identification (ENV-06) plus altitudinal vegetation zones, which is GEO-16.

questions.stem: Atal Innovation Mission is set up under the
options: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship
questions.explanation_md:
**Atal Innovation Mission (AIM) is set up under NITI Aayog** (announced in Budget 2015-16, flagship umbrella for innovation and entrepreneurship).

Its components, worth remembering as a set:
- **Atal Tinkering Labs (ATL)** — in schools, class 6 upward
- **Atal Incubation Centres (AIC)** and **Established Incubation Centres**
- **Atal New India Challenges / ARISE** — product innovation with ministries and MSMEs
- **Atal Community Innovation Centres (ACIC)** — in unserved/underserved regions

Don't confuse with **AGNIi** (Accelerating Growth of New India's Innovations, under the PSA's office) or the **Atal Pension Yojana** (Ministry of Finance/PFRDA).
questions.tagging_note: No topic covers Atal Innovation Mission by name. The discriminating fact is that AIM sits inside NITI Aayog, so POL-25 (which names NITI Aayog) is the sharpest retrieval path; SNT-14 (S&T missions and institutions) and CAI-10 (schemes tracker) are the plausible alternative homes. Subject boundary here is genuinely soft between POL, SNT and CAI.

questions.stem: On 21st June, the Sun
options: does not set below the horizon at the Arctic Circle
does not set below the horizon at Antarctic Circle
shines vertically overhead at noon on the Equator
shines vertically overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn
questions.explanation_md:
21 June is the **summer solstice for the Northern Hemisphere**: the Sun is vertically overhead at noon on the **Tropic of Cancer (23½° N)**, and the entire area from the **Arctic Circle (66½° N) to the North Pole has 24-hour daylight** — the midnight sun.

Checking each option:
- **(a) Correct — at the Arctic Circle on 21 June the Sun does not set below the horizon.** This is the definition of the Arctic Circle: the lowest latitude with one full day of midnight sun.
- (b) Wrong — the **Antarctic Circle** is in 24-hour *darkness* on 21 June (its polar night); the Sun does not *rise* there.
- (c) Wrong — the Sun is overhead at the Equator only on the **equinoxes, 21 March and 23 September**.
- (d) Wrong — overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn on 22 December**, the winter solstice.

**Arctic Circle → midnight sun on 21 June; Antarctic Circle → midnight sun on 22 December.**

questions.stem: Which one of the following groups of plants was domesticated in the 'New World' and introduced into the 'Old World'?
questions.explanation_md:
**New World (Americas) domesticates: tobacco, cocoa, rubber, maize, potato, tomato, chilli, cotton (some species), groundnut, pineapple, cashew, tapioca.**

Check each option:
- **(a) Tobacco, cocoa, rubber** — all three are American. Tobacco (*Nicotiana*, Andes/Mesoamerica), cocoa (*Theobroma cacao*, Amazon/Mesoamerica), rubber (*Hevea brasiliensis*, Amazon). Correct.
- (b) has cotton — the *cultivated* cottons include Old World species (*G. arboreum*, *G. herbaceum*, domesticated in India/Africa), so cotton is not exclusively New World.
- (c) coffee (Ethiopia) and sugarcane (New Guinea/SE Asia) are Old World.
- (d) coffee and wheat (Fertile Crescent) are Old World.

Only (a) has all three from the Americas.
questions.tagging_note: Columbian exchange — origin/domestication of crops (tobacco, cocoa, rubber) and their transfer to the Old World. The vocabulary has no topic for world history/economic botany or crop origins; GEO-23 (world economic geography — agriculture) is the closest genuine fit, with GEO-17 only for the crop-knowledge overlap. Real gap: crop origins / Columbian exchange is not covered by any topic.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Asiatic lion is naturally found in India only.
2. Double-humped camel is naturally found in India only.
3. One-horned rhinoceros is naturally found in India only.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — Correct.** The Asiatic lion (*Panthera leo persica*) survives in the wild **only in Gir, Gujarat**. Its historic range (Persia, Mesopotamia) is extinct.

**Statement 2 — Incorrect.** The double-humped Bactrian camel is found in Nubra valley (Ladakh) in India, but **also naturally in Mongolia, China and Central Asia** — the wild Bactrian camel's core range. Not India only.

**Statement 3 — Incorrect.** The greater one-horned rhino (*Rhinoceros unicornis*) is found in Assam and West Bengal, but **also in Nepal (Chitwan) and Bhutan**. Not India only.

Only 1 → **(a)**.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Famous place* | *River* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Pandharpur | Chandrabhaga |
| 2. Tiruchirappalli | Cauvery |
| 3. Hampi | Malaprabha |

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
**Pair 1 — Correct.** Pandharpur (Solapur, Maharashtra), the Vithoba temple town, stands on the **Bhima river, locally called Chandrabhaga** because it curves like a half-moon.

**Pair 2 — Correct.** Tiruchirappalli (Rockfort, Srirangam) lies on the **Cauvery**; Srirangam is the island between the Cauvery and Kollidam.

**Pair 3 — Incorrect.** **Hampi (Vijayanagara) is on the Tungabhadra, not the Malaprabha.** The Malaprabha flows past **Badami–Aihole–Pattadakal** (Chalukyan sites) — that is the trap.

1 and 2 only → **(a)**.
questions.tagging_note: Famous place–river pairs; tested knowledge is Peninsular drainage (Bhima/Chandrabhaga, Cauvery, Tungabhadra) plus atlas placement. Format follows the house convention that 'consider the following pairs ... correctly matched' is tagged `pairs` (as in 2018 Q37/Q64/Q90).

questions.stem: In a given year in India, official poverty lines are higher in some States than in others because
options: poverty rates vary from State to State
price levels vary from State to State
Gross State Product varies from State to State
quality of public distribution varies from State to State
questions.explanation_md:
A poverty line is a **money value of a fixed basket of goods** (calorie norm plus non-food essentials). The same basket costs different amounts in different States, so the rupee line differs.

**State-specific poverty lines are derived from State-level price levels (Tendulkar/Rangarajan use State-wise price differentials and separate rural/urban lines).**

- (a) reverses cause and effect — the poverty *rate* is the output, computed after the line is fixed.
- (c) GSDP is an income aggregate, not an input to the line.
- (d) PDS quality does not enter the line's construction.

Answer: **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Core is poverty-line construction (ECO-17); ECO-09 is genuine because the answer turns on inter-State price levels / cost-of-living indices.

questions.stem: In the context of which of the following do some scientists suggest the use of cirrus cloud thinning technique and the injection of sulphate aerosol into stratosphere?
options: Creating the artificial rains in some regions
Reducing the frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones
Reducing the adverse effects of solar wind on the Earth
questions.explanation_md:
Both are **geoengineering / climate-intervention** proposals aimed at cooling the planet:

- **Stratospheric aerosol injection** — sulphate particles in the stratosphere reflect incoming sunlight back to space (mimics a volcanic eruption like Pinatubo 1991, which cooled Earth ~0.5°C). This is *solar radiation management*.
- **Cirrus cloud thinning** — thin high cirrus clouds trap outgoing longwave radiation; seeding them so ice crystals grow larger and fall out lets **more heat escape to space**. This is longwave/terrestrial radiation management.

**Both are proposed to counter global warming, not to make rain, weaken cyclones or block solar wind.**

Answer: **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: Solar geoengineering (stratospheric aerosol injection, cirrus cloud thinning) to counter global warming. No topic names geoengineering explicitly; ENV-12 (radiative forcing, feedbacks) is the nearest genuine home, ENV-13 covers it only as a climate-response debate.

questions.stem: In the context of which one of the following are the terms 'pyrolysis and plasma gasification' mentioned?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both are thermal waste-to-energy conversion routes.**

- **Pyrolysis** — heating organic/municipal waste in the **absence of oxygen** (~400–800°C) to yield syngas, bio-oil and char.
- **Plasma gasification** — an electric plasma arc at very high temperature (several thousand °C) breaks waste into syngas and an inert vitrified slag; used for hazardous and municipal solid waste.

Along with incineration, these are the standard WTE technologies discussed for Indian MSW management.

Answer: **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: Waste-to-energy technologies — sits between solid-waste management (ENV-11) and alternative energy (ENV-16), consistent with how 2023 Q55 and 2024 Q46 waste questions were split.

questions.stem: Which of the following are in Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve?
options: Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney Wildlife Sanctuaries; and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve
Mudumalai, Sathyamangalam and Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuaries; and Silent Valley National Park
Kaundinya, Gundla Brahmeswaram and Papikonda Wildlife Sanctuaries; and Mukurthi National Park
Kawal and Sri Venkateswara Wildlife Sanctuaries; and Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve
questions.explanation_md:
**Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve straddles the Kerala–Tamil Nadu border at the southern tip of the Western Ghats** (added to UNESCO's World Network in 2016).

Its constituents: **Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney Wildlife Sanctuaries (Kerala) and Kalakad–Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve (Tamil Nadu)**, plus Achankovil forests.

Why the others fail:
- (b) Mudumalai/Sathyamangalam/Wayanad/Silent Valley = **Nilgiri** Biosphere Reserve.
- (c) Kaundinya, Gundla Brahmeswaram, Papikonda are Andhra sanctuaries; Mukurthi is in the Nilgiris — not one reserve.
- (d) Kawal, Sri Venkateswara, Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam are Telangana/Andhra — not Agasthyamalai.

Answer: **(a)**.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Some species of turtles are herbivores.
2. Some species of fish are herbivores.
3. Some species of marine mammals are herbivores.
4. Some species of snakes are viviparous.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Statement 1 — Correct.** Adult **green sea turtles** are largely herbivorous (seagrass, algae); many tortoises/terrapins are herbivorous too.

**Statement 2 — Correct.** Herbivorous fish are common — **parrotfish, surgeonfish, grass carp** graze algae and plants.

**Statement 3 — Correct.** **Dugongs and manatees (Sirenia) are fully herbivorous marine mammals** — the dugong grazes seagrass in the Gulf of Mannar and Andamans. This is the statement candidates wrongly reject.

**Statement 4 — Correct.** Many snakes are **viviparous / ovoviviparous** — sea snakes, boas, most vipers (including Russell's viper give live birth).

All four correct → **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects: statements 1–3 are trophic level / feeding habit (ENV-01 food chains), statement 4 is animal reproduction (viviparity), which belongs to general zoology. SNT-01 is 'basic biology — cell, genetics, human systems, nutrition' and does not really cover comparative animal biology, so the viviparity half of this question has no clean home in the syllabus tree.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Wildlife* | *Naturally found in* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Blue-finned Mahseer | Cauvery River |
| 2. Irrawaddy Dolphin | Chambal River |
| 3. Rusty-spotted Cat | Eastern Ghats |

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
**Pair 1 — Correct.** The **blue-finned/ hump-backed Mahseer (*Tor khudree* / *Tor remadevii*) is endemic to the Cauvery** system, iconic of the Cauvery angling reaches.

**Pair 2 — Incorrect.** The **Irrawaddy dolphin in India occurs in Chilika Lake (Odisha)** and coastal brackish waters, not the Chambal. **The Chambal's cetacean is the Gangetic river dolphin**, along with gharial — that is the trap.

**Pair 3 — Correct.** The **rusty-spotted cat**, the world's smallest wild cat, occurs in the dry deciduous forests and scrub of central and peninsular India including the **Eastern Ghats** (Andhra, Odisha, Gujarat, MP).

1 and 3 only → **(c)**.

questions.stem: Why is there a great concern about the 'microbeads' that are released into environment?
options: They are considered harmful to marine ecosystems.
They are considered to cause skin cancer in children.
They are small enough to be absorbed by crop plants in irrigated fields.
They are often found to be used as food adulterants.
questions.explanation_md:
**Microbeads are tiny solid plastic particles (<5 mm, usually polyethylene/polypropylene) added to face scrubs, toothpaste and cosmetics.** They pass straight through sewage treatment plants into rivers and the sea.

There they are **ingested by plankton, fish and filter feeders, block digestion, and adsorb persistent organic pollutants that then biomagnify up the marine food chain** — hence bans (US Microbead-Free Waters Act 2015; UK 2018).

The concern is ecological, not dermatological (b), agronomic (c) or adulteration (d).

Answer: **(a)**.
questions.tagging_note: Microplastics/microbeads — pollution (ENV-11) with a genuine marine-ecosystem impact angle (ENV-04).

questions.stem: Recently, there was a growing awareness in our country about the importance of Himalayan nettle (*Girardinia diversifolia*) because it is found to be a sustainable source of
questions.explanation_md:
**Girardinia diversifolia — the Himalayan giant nettle — yields a strong bast fibre, known as *allo* in Uttarakhand and Nepal.** The stem bark is retted, boiled with wood ash, beaten and spun into yarn for shawls, bags, jackets and rope.

Why it got attention: it grows wild at 1,200–3,000 m without cultivation inputs, is harvested annually without killing the plant, and has become a livelihood product for hill women's SHGs (Uttarakhand Bamboo & Fibre Development Board, and similar work in Sikkim/Manipur) — a *sustainable* textile fibre, which is the exact word in the stem.

Eliminate the rest: no anti-malarial is sourced from it (that is *Artemisia annua*); biodiesel comes from oil-bearing seeds like jatropha, karanja, mahua — nettle is not an oilseed; and it is harvested in small hill quantities, far too little for paper pulp.
questions.tagging_note: Species-in-news item about a plant PRODUCT (bast fibre for textiles), not about ecology or conservation status. The tree has no economic-botany / plant-products topic — ENV-07 (Indian flora and fauna) is the only species bucket available, matching the precedent set for Prosopis juliflora (2018 Q86) and Red Sanders (2016 Q53).

questions.stem:
For the measurement/estimation of which of the following are satellite images/remote sensing data used?
1. Chlorophyll content in the vegetation of a specific location
2. Greenhouse gas emissions from rice paddies of a specific location
3. Land surface temperatures of a specific location
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
All three — remote sensing is not just photographs, it is measurement across the electromagnetic spectrum.

**1. Chlorophyll — correct.** Chlorophyll absorbs red and strongly reflects near-infrared. That contrast is the whole basis of NDVI; hyperspectral sensors and Sentinel-2's red-edge bands give actual chlorophyll concentration.

**2. GHG from rice paddies — correct.** Two routes: (i) satellites map paddy extent and the flooding/inundation regime (microwave SAR sees water under the canopy), which is fed into methane emission models; (ii) atmospheric sounders — GOSAT, Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI — measure the CH₄ column directly.

**3. Land surface temperature — correct.** Thermal infrared sensors (Landsat TIRS, MODIS, INSAT-3D) measure emitted long-wave radiation; this is how urban heat islands are mapped.

Elimination shortcut: statement 1 is unarguably true, which kills options (b) and (c); statement 3 is unarguably true, which kills (a). **Only (d) survives without needing a verdict on 2.**
questions.tagging_note: GAP: no topic in the vocabulary covers remote sensing / satellite imagery / GIS applications. SNT-05 is titled 'Space — ISRO missions, launch vehicles, NavIC, private space sector' — it holds the satellites but teaches nothing about what sensors can measure; SNT-13 is added only for its 'sensors' clause. Statement 2 (methane from paddies) also brushes ENV-12, but the thing actually tested is remote-sensing capability, not GHG chemistry. Worth a dedicated remote-sensing/GIS topic.

questions.stem:
Consider the following States :
1. Chhattisgarh
2. Madhya Pradesh
3. Maharashtra
4. Odisha
With reference to the States mentioned above, in terms of percentage of forest cover to the total area of State, which one of the following is the correct ascending order?
questions.explanation_md:
Percentage of forest cover to State geographical area (ISFR figures current in 2019):

| State | Forest cover | % of State area |
|---|---|---|
| Maharashtra | ~50,700 km² | **~16.5%** |
| Madhya Pradesh | ~77,400 km² | **~25.1%** |
| Odisha | ~51,300 km² | **~33.0%** |
| Chhattisgarh | ~55,500 km² | **~41.1%** |

Ascending: **Maharashtra → Madhya Pradesh → Odisha → Chhattisgarh = 3-2-4-1**, option (c).

The trap is confusing *absolute area* with *percentage*. MP has the largest forest area in India in km², but it is also a huge State (3.08 lakh km²), so its percentage is modest. Odisha and Chhattisgarh are compact and heavily forested, so they top the percentage list. Maharashtra, with almost the same geographical area as MP but less forest, is last.

Anchor to remember: **Chhattisgarh ~41% > Odisha ~33% > MP ~25% > Maharashtra ~16%.**
questions.tagging_note: Pure ISFR data recall — state-wise percentage forest cover ranked in ascending order. No topic covers environmental statistics/reports; GEO-16 (India — natural vegetation and forest types) is the shelf where forest-cover data would be revised, ENV-03 added for the forests-as-ecosystem straddle. Format is 'simple' (four plain ordering choices), following the 2021 Q45 ascending-sequence precedent.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements are correct about the deposits of 'methane hydrate'?
1. Global warming might trigger the release of methane gas from these deposits.
2. Large deposits of 'methane hydrate' are found in Arctic Tundra and under the seafloor.
3. Methane in atmosphere oxidizes to carbon dioxide after a decade or two.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
Methane hydrate = methane molecules trapped in a cage of ice, stable only under **high pressure and low temperature**.

**1. Correct.** That stability is the point — warming permafrost or warming ocean bottom water destabilises the cage and releases CH₄. This is the feared "clathrate gun" positive feedback: CH₄ is ~25× CO₂ over 100 years, so release causes more warming, which releases more.

**2. Correct.** Exactly the two settings where the pressure–temperature window exists: **Arctic permafrost/tundra, and continental-margin seafloor sediments** (India's own deposits are in the Krishna–Godavari, Mahanadi and Andaman basins, surveyed under the National Gas Hydrate Programme).

**3. Correct.** Atmospheric methane's residence time is roughly **9–12 years**; it is destroyed mainly by hydroxyl (OH) radicals in the troposphere and ends up as CO₂ and water vapour. "A decade or two" fits. This is why methane is a short-lived but potent climate forcer — cutting CH₄ gives fast temperature benefit.

All three correct → (d).
questions.tagging_note: Straddles ENV and GEO: statements 1 and 3 are climate-feedback and atmospheric-lifetime science (ENV-12), statement 2 is occurrence of gas hydrates as an unconventional energy deposit (GEO-18, mineral and energy resources).

questions.stem:
Consider the following :
1. Carbon monoxide
2. Methane
3. Ozone
4. Sulphur dioxide
Which of the above are released into atmosphere due to the burning of crop/biomass residue?
questions.explanation_md:
Crop-residue (stubble) burning is *incomplete* combustion of biomass, so it emits far more than CO₂.

- **1. Carbon monoxide — yes.** The signature product of oxygen-starved smouldering combustion.
- **2. Methane — yes.** Also released by incomplete combustion; burning 1 tonne of paddy straw releases roughly 3 kg of particulate matter, 60 kg CO, 1,460 kg CO₂ and 2 kg SO₂ (widely quoted IARI figures).
- **4. Sulphur dioxide — yes.** Plant tissue contains sulphur, which oxidises to SO₂.
- **3. Ozone — the only debatable one.** O₃ is not emitted directly; it is a *secondary* pollutant formed when the NOx and volatile organic compounds in the smoke react in sunlight. UPSC counts it, and standard MoEFCC/IARI listings of stubble-burning pollutants include ozone.

**Decide it by the options, not by the ozone debate: 1, 2 and 4 are certainly released, and no option reads "1, 2 and 4 only" — so (d) is forced.** That elimination is the safe route in the hall.
questions.tagging_note: Primarily air pollution from open biomass/stubble burning (ENV-11); ENV-12 included because CO, CH4 and O3 are also GHG/short-lived climate pollutants. GEO-17 (agriculture practice) was considered and rejected — the question asks about emitted species, not cropping practice.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Sea* | *Bordering country* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Adriatic Sea | Albania |
| 2. Black Sea | Croatia |
| 3. Caspian Sea | Kazakhstan |
| 4. Mediterranean Sea | Morocco |
| 5. Red Sea | Syria |

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
- **1. Adriatic Sea – Albania: CORRECT.** Albania's western coast is Adriatic (its south-west turns into the Ionian at the Strait of Otranto). Adriatic littorals: Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia & Herzegovina (a tiny Neum strip), Montenegro, Albania.
- **2. Black Sea – Croatia: WRONG. Croatia is on the Adriatic, not the Black Sea.** Black Sea littorals are only six: Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia, Georgia.
- **3. Caspian Sea – Kazakhstan: CORRECT.** The five Caspian States: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Azerbaijan.
- **4. Mediterranean Sea – Morocco: CORRECT.** Morocco has two coasts — Atlantic in the west and Mediterranean in the north, across the Strait of Gibraltar from Spain.
- **5. Red Sea – Syria: WRONG. Syria is on the Mediterranean.** Red Sea littorals: Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Israel and Jordan (at the Gulf of Aqaba).

Correct pairs = **1, 3 and 4 only** → (b). Two clean eliminations (Croatia, Syria) settle it without needing any option-juggling.

questions.stem: Among the following, which one is the largest exporter of rice in the world in the last five years?
questions.explanation_md:
**India has been the world's largest rice exporter continuously since 2012**, when it lifted its ban on non-basmati exports and overtook Thailand. Exports have run around 10–12 million tonnes a year — roughly a quarter of all rice traded globally — split between basmati (chiefly to Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE) and non-basmati (Bangladesh, Nepal, Benin and West Africa).

Rule out the others:
- **China** is the world's largest *producer* and also a large *importer* — it consumes almost everything it grows. Producer ≠ exporter is the classic trap here.
- **Thailand** (not offered) and **Vietnam** are ranked 2nd/3rd, at roughly 5–7 mt each.
- **Myanmar** exports only ~2–3 mt.

Carry the pair: **India = largest exporter; China = largest producer and consumer.**
questions.tagging_note: World-comparative agri-trade fact whose answer is India. Tagged GEO-17 primary to match the 2025 Q24 turmeric precedent (India-as-largest-producer/exporter facts revised under India agriculture); GEO-23 added for the world economic-geography framing. ECO-12 (external sector/trade) was considered and rejected — no trade mechanism is tested, only a rank fact.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| *Glacier* | *River* |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Bandarpunch | Yamuna |
| 2. Bara Shigri | Chenab |
| 3. Milam | Mandakini |
| 4. Siachen | Nubra |
| 5. Zemu | Manas |

Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
- **1. Bandarpunch – Yamuna: CORRECT.** The Yamunotri glacier sits on the Bandarpunch massif in Uttarkashi; the Yamuna rises there.
- **2. Bara Shigri – Chenab: CORRECT.** Himachal's largest glacier, in the Lahaul–Spiti Chandra valley. It feeds the Chandra, which meets the Bhaga at Tandi to form the Chandrabhaga — the **Chenab**.
- **3. Milam – Mandakini: WRONG.** The Milam glacier in Pithoragarh (Kumaon) is the source of the **Gori Ganga**, a Kali/Sharda tributary. **The Mandakini rises from the Chorabari glacier above Kedarnath.**
- **4. Siachen – Nubra: CORRECT.** Meltwater from the Siachen glacier forms the Nubra, which joins the Shyok, a Indus tributary.
- **5. Zemu – Manas: WRONG.** The Zemu glacier on Kanchenjunga's east flank in Sikkim feeds the **Teesta**. The Manas rises in Bhutan/southern Tibet and has nothing to do with Zemu.

Correct = **1, 2 and 4** → (a). Since options (c) and (d) both need pair 5, knowing Zemu → Teesta alone reduces the question to (a) vs (b), and Milam → Gori Ganga finishes it.
questions.tagging_note: Glacier-to-source-river pairing: drainage (GEO-13) is the tested link, Himalayan physiography/glacier location (GEO-12) supports it. Same pattern as the 2024 Q9 waterfall-river pairs.

questions.stem: In India, the use of carbofuran, methyl parathion, phorate and triazophos is viewed with apprehension. These chemicals are used as
questions.explanation_md:
**All four are insecticides — three of them (methyl parathion, phorate, triazophos) are organophosphates and carbofuran is a carbamate.** Both classes work by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which is why they are equally toxic to humans, birds and bees, not just to the target pest.

The apprehension in India: these are **highly hazardous pesticides**, most of them WHO Class Ia/Ib "extremely/highly hazardous". The Anupam Verma Committee reviewed 66 pesticides banned elsewhere but still used here and recommended phasing several out; the Ministry of Agriculture's 2018 and 2020 draft orders proposed banning carbofuran, methyl parathion, phorate and triazophos among dozens of others. Carbofuran in particular is notorious for mass poisoning of birds — it has been used to deliberately poison raptors and, abroad, big cats.

The other options do not fit: preservatives, ripening agents (that would be calcium carbide/ethylene) and cosmetic moisturisers are entirely different chemistry.
questions.tagging_note: No topic covers agro-chemicals / pesticides as such. ENV-11 (pollution — soil, water, standards) carries the 'viewed with apprehension' toxicity angle these organophosphate and carbamate compounds are known for; SNT-13 (everyday chemistry) is the fallback identification bucket, following the 2017 Q73 precedent. GEO-17 (agricultural inputs) is a weaker third fit and was left out.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Under Ramsar Convention, it is mandatory on the part of the Government of India to protect and conserve all the wetlands in the territory of India.
2. The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010 were framed by the Government of India based on the recommendations of Ramsar Convention.
3. The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010 also encompass the drainage area or catchment regions of the wetlands as determined by the authority.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**1. WRONG.** The Ramsar Convention obliges a Contracting Party to designate **at least one** wetland for the List of Wetlands of International Importance, to promote its "wise use" and to conserve listed sites — it does **not** make protection of *all* wetlands in the territory mandatory. Ramsar is a framework treaty with national discretion, not a binding blanket obligation. The word "all" is the giveaway.

**2. WRONG.** **The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010 were notified by the Centre under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** — India's own domestic law — prompted by the National Environment Policy, 2006 and judicial direction, not framed "based on the recommendations of the Ramsar Convention." Ramsar issues guidance, not recommendations that States then legislate on. (These Rules were later replaced by the Wetlands Rules, 2017, which decentralised regulation to State Wetlands Authorities.)

**3. CORRECT.** The 2010 Rules explicitly extended beyond the water body itself: the definition covered **the drainage area or catchment region of the wetland as determined by the authority** — recognising that a wetland cannot be protected while its catchment is degraded.

Only 3 is correct → (c). Statement 1 alone eliminates (a) and (d); the fate of statement 2 then decides between (b) and (c).
questions.tagging_note: Ramsar obligations (ENV-14, per the 2014 Q2 and Q10 precedent) plus the domestic Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2010, which sit across ENV-04 (wetlands) and ENV-09 (environmental laws).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Agricultural soils release nitrogen oxides into environment.
2. Cattle release ammonia into environment.
3. Poultry industry releases reactive nitrogen compounds into environment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are sources of reactive nitrogen (Nr).**

1. **Correct** — nitrogen fertiliser on agricultural soils undergoes nitrification/denitrification, releasing **N₂O and NO**. Agriculture is India's largest single source of N₂O.
2. **Correct** — urea in cattle urine and dung is hydrolysed by urease to **ammonia (NH₃)**. Livestock is the single biggest NH₃ source in India.
3. **Correct** — poultry litter volatilises ammonia; the *Indian Nitrogen Assessment (2017)* flagged poultry as one of the fastest-growing Nr sources.

Since 1, 2 and 3 all hold, the answer is **(d)**. Note the trap: nitrogen oxides ≠ ammonia, but **both are "reactive nitrogen"** — only inert N₂ is not.

questions.stem: What is common to the places known as Aliyar, Isapur and Kangsabati?
questions.explanation_md:
**All three are dams/reservoirs** — (d).

- **Aliyar** — dam in Coimbatore district, **Tamil Nadu** (Parambikulam–Aliyar Project).
- **Isapur** — dam on the **Penganga** river, Nanded/Yavatmal, **Maharashtra**.
- **Kangsabati (Kansai)** — reservoir in **West Bengal** (Mukutmanipur, Bankura), at the Kangsabati–Kumari confluence.

Elimination works even without recall: uranium in India is Jaduguda/Tummalapalle, and no tropical rainforest or cave-system group carries these names.
questions.tagging_note: Aliyar (TN), Isapur (Maharashtra) and Kangsabati (West Bengal) are all water reservoirs/dams. Pure place-recall; the vocabulary has no dedicated 'dams and reservoirs of India' topic, so it sits between India drainage (GEO-13) and the atlas/places-in-news drill (GEO-24).

questions.stem:
In the context of proposals to the use of hydrogen-enriched CNG (H-CNG) as fuel for buses in public transport, consider the following statements :
1. The main advantage of the use of H-CNG is the elimination of carbon monoxide emissions.
2. H-CNG as fuel reduces carbon dioxide and hydrocarbon emissions.
3. Hydrogen up to one-fifth by volume can be blended with CNG as fuel for buses.
4. H-CNG makes the fuel less expensive than CNG.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**(b) 2 and 3 only.**

1. **Wrong** — H-CNG *reduces* CO by roughly 70%, but hydrogen blending does **not eliminate** carbon monoxide; the CNG fraction still contains carbon. "Elimination" is the giveaway word.
2. **Correct** — better, leaner combustion cuts **CO₂, unburnt hydrocarbons and CO**.
3. **Correct** — **hydrogen up to ~18–20% (one-fifth) by volume** is the blend limit; beyond that engine knocking and NOₓ rise. Delhi's DTC trial used 18% H-CNG from IOCL's Faridabad compact reforming plant.
4. **Wrong** — hydrogen production adds cost, so **H-CNG is dearer than CNG**, not cheaper.
questions.tagging_note: H-CNG is a hydrogen fuel-blend question; SNT-12 (energy technology — hydrogen) is the closest fit, with an emissions/air-pollution angle (ENV-11). ENV-16 (green hydrogen missions) was rejected because the question is about fuel chemistry and emissions, not policy.

questions.stem: Why are dewdrops **not** formed on a cloudy night?
options: Clouds absorb the radiation released from the Earth's surface.
Clouds reflect back the Earth's radiation.
The Earth's surface would have low temperature on cloudy nights.
Clouds deflect the blowing wind to ground level.
questions.explanation_md:
**(b)** Dew forms only when the ground cools below the dew point by **terrestrial radiation on a clear, calm night**.

Clouds act as a blanket: they **absorb and re-radiate (reflect back) the Earth's outgoing longwave radiation**, so the surface stays warm and never reaches the dew point — no condensation.

Why the others fail: (c) inverts the physics — cloudy nights are **warmer**, not colder, at the surface; (a) is only half the mechanism and, without the re-radiation back down, would not keep the ground warm; (d) is irrelevant — in fact wind *prevents* dew by mixing the air.

Ideal dew conditions: clear sky, calm air, high relative humidity, long winter night.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles insolation/terrestrial radiation and heat budget (GEO-06) and condensation forms such as dew (GEO-08); the answer turns on radiation, so GEO-06 is primary.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The 44th Amendment to the Constitution of India introduced an Article placing the election of the Prime Minister beyond judicial review.
2. The Supreme Court of India struck down the 99th Amendment to the Constitution of India as being violative of the independence of judiciary.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**(b) 2 only.**

1. **Wrong — wrong amendment.** It was the **39th Amendment (1975)** that inserted **Article 329A**, putting the election of the PM and Speaker beyond judicial review (post-*Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain*). The **44th Amendment (1978)** did the opposite — it **repealed Article 329A** and restored judicial review.
2. **Correct** — in *Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India* (**2015, NJAC case**) the Court struck down the **99th Amendment** and the NJAC Act as violating **independence of the judiciary**, a basic-structure feature, and revived the collegium.

Remember the pair: **39th = shield, 44th = repeal.**
questions.tagging_note: Tests specific amendments (39th vs 44th) and the NJAC/99th Amendment judgment — amendment history (POL-12) plus basic structure/landmark judgments (POL-13) and judicial independence (POL-20).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The motion to impeach a Judge of the Supreme Court of India cannot be rejected by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha as per the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
2. The Constitution of India defines and gives details of what constitutes 'incapacity and proved misbehaviour' of the Judges of the Supreme Court of India.
3. The details of the process of impeachment of the Judges of the Supreme Court of India are given in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
4. If the motion for the impeachment of a Judge is taken up for voting, the law requires the motion to be backed by each House of the Parliament and supported by a majority of total membership of that House and by not less than two-thirds of total members of that House present and voting.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**(c) 3 and 4 only.**

1. **Wrong** — under **Section 3(1) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968** the Speaker/Chairman, after consulting whomever he thinks fit, **may admit or *refuse to admit* the motion**. Chairman Venkaiah Naidu's 2018 rejection of the motion against CJI Dipak Misra is the live example.
2. **Wrong** — the Constitution uses "**proved misbehaviour or incapacity**" (Art. 124(4)) but **nowhere defines** either term.
3. **Correct** — the Constitution gives only the removal ground and the majority; the **procedure** (motion, three-member inquiry committee, report) is in the **Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968**.
4. **Correct** — Art. 124(4) special majority: **each House separately**, by a **majority of the total membership** *and* **not less than two-thirds of members present and voting**.

questions.stem: The Ninth Schedule was introduced in the Constitution of India during the prime ministership of
questions.explanation_md:
**(a) Jawaharlal Nehru.**

The **Ninth Schedule** was added by the **First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951** (along with Art. 31A and 31B), to protect **zamindari abolition and land-reform laws** from being struck down for violating Fundamental Rights.

Article **31B** gives the shield. But in **I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)** the Supreme Court held that any law placed in the Ninth Schedule **after 24 April 1973** (the *Kesavananda* date) is open to challenge if it damages the **basic structure**.
questions.tagging_note: Ninth Schedule came in via the 1st Amendment (1951, Nehru). Fact lives partly in the schedules list (POL-03, Laxmikanth Ch.3) and partly in the history of significant amendments (POL-12, Ch.10); no topic is specifically 'Schedules of the Constitution'.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Coal sector was nationalized by the Government of India under Indira Gandhi.
2. Now, coal blocks are allocated on lottery basis.
3. Till recently, India imported coal to meet the shortages of domestic supply, but now India is self-sufficient in coal production.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**(a) 1 only.**

1. **Correct** — nationalisation happened under **Indira Gandhi**: coking coal in **1971–72** and non-coking coal in **1973** (Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, 1973), leading to **Coal India Ltd (1975)**.
2. **Wrong** — after the Supreme Court cancelled 204 blocks in **2014**, the **Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015** made allocation by **auction/e-auction (competitive bidding)**, not lottery.
3. **Wrong** — India remains among the **world's largest coal importers** (coking coal especially, which India lacks in quality). Self-sufficiency is a target, not a fact.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects: coal reserves/production/imports is GEO-18 (mineral and energy resources), while nationalisation and block-allocation policy is energy-sector economics (ECO-16). Tagged GEO primary because the decisive statement is about domestic coal supply.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 exempts several posts from disqualification on the grounds of 'Office of Profit'.
2. The above-mentioned Act was amended five times.
3. The term 'Office of Profit' is well-defined in the Constitution of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**(a) 1 and 2 only.**

1. **Correct** — the **Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959** lists offices exempted from disqualification under **Art. 102(1)(a) / 191(1)(a)**.
2. **Treated as correct** — the Act has been amended several times, notably the **2006 amendment** (retrospective, exempting the National Advisory Council chair and others, after the Jaya Bachchan / Sonia Gandhi episode).
3. **Wrong — this is the decider.** "**Office of profit**" is **used but nowhere defined** in the Constitution; its content comes from judicial tests (who appoints/removes, whether remuneration or pecuniary gain flows, control over the office).

Even if statement 2's exact count is uncertain, 1 is right and 3 is wrong, so **(a)** is the only option that survives.
questions.tagging_note: Office of Profit disqualification of MPs is Laxmikanth Ch.22 (POL-18); the disqualification-of-members angle also touches POL-26.

questions.stem: Under which Schedule of the Constitution of India can the transfer of tribal land to private parties for mining be declared null and void?
questions.explanation_md:
**(b) Fifth Schedule.**

The Fifth Schedule governs **Scheduled Areas** in states other than the North-East. Under it the **Governor** may, by regulation, **prohibit or restrict the transfer of land by or among Scheduled Tribes**, and may repeal or amend any Parliament/State law in its application to a Scheduled Area.

This is the basis of ***Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh* (1997)**, where the Supreme Court held that **transfer of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private mining companies is null and void** — mining leases there can go only to the State, a State undertaking, or a tribal cooperative.

Quick discard: Third = oaths, Ninth = laws immune from FR challenge, Twelfth = municipalities (74th Amendment).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) in India :
1. PVTGs reside in 18 States and one Union Territory.
2. A stagnant or declining population is one of the criteria for determining PVTG status.
3. There are 95 PVTGs officially notified in the country so far.
4. Irular and Konda Reddi tribes are included in the list of PVTGs.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: 1, 2 and 4.**

- **(1) Correct** — PVTGs are spread over **18 States + the UT of Andaman & Nicobar Islands**.
- **(2) Correct** — The four Dhebar-Committee-derived criteria are: pre-agricultural level of technology, low level of literacy, economic backwardness, and a **stagnant or declining population**.
- **(3) Wrong** — The notified number is **75, not 95**. This is the single fact that kills options (a), (b) and (d).
- **(4) Correct** — *Irular* (Tamil Nadu/Kerala) and *Konda Reddi* (Andhra Pradesh/Telangana) are both on the PVTG list.

Memory hook: **75 PVTGs, 18 States + 1 UT**. Odisha has the most (13).
questions.tagging_note: PVTG identification criteria and the notified list are executive/tribal-welfare facts (Ministry of Tribal Affairs), not constitutional text. The vocabulary has no dedicated social-justice / tribal-welfare or vulnerable-sections topic; POL-23 (Scheduled & Tribal Areas) is the nearest home and POL-24 covers NCST. Genuine gap in the syllabus tree for schemes and welfare of vulnerable sections.

questions.stem: With reference to the Constitution of India, prohibitions or limitations or provisions contained in ordinary laws cannot act as prohibitions or limitations on the constitutional powers under Article 142. It could mean which one of the following?
options: The decisions taken by the Election Commission of India while discharging its duties cannot be challenged in any court of law.
The Supreme Court of India is not constrained in the exercise of its powers by laws made by the Parliament.
In the event of grave financial crisis in the country, the President of India can declare Financial Emergency without the counsel from the Cabinet.
State Legislatures cannot make laws on certain matters without the concurrence of Union Legislature.
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (b).**

**Article 142 gives the Supreme Court power to pass any decree/order necessary for "complete justice"** in a case before it. The quoted line — that ordinary-law prohibitions cannot limit Article 142 — means exactly that the **SC's constitutional power is not fettered by statutes made by Parliament** (Union Carbide, Supreme Court Bar Assn. v. Union of India).

Why the others fail:
- (a) Election Commission — Art. 324; its orders *are* judicially reviewable, and Art. 329 bars only election-petition-type challenges.
- (c) Financial Emergency — Art. 360, and the President always acts on Cabinet advice (Art. 74).
- (d) Concurrence of Union legislature — Art. 254(2)/249 territory, nothing to do with Art. 142.
questions.transcription_note: Options span both columns on page 23: (a) at foot of left column, (b)-(d) at head of right column. Verified all four present and in order.

questions.stem:
With reference to the Legislative Assembly of a State in India, consider the following statements :
1. The Governor makes a customary address to Members of the House at the commencement of the first session of the year.
2. When a State Legislature does not have a rule on a particular matter, it follows the Lok Sabha rule on that matter.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (c) Both 1 and 2**

**Statement 1 — correct (Article 176).**
Article 176(1) requires the Governor to address the Legislative Assembly (or both Houses assembled together, in a bicameral State) at the commencement of the first session after each general election *and* at the commencement of the first session of each year. Statement 1 claims exactly the second of those two occasions, with the exact quantifier: the **first** session of the year, not every session and not every sitting. That is the standard trap on this Article, and the statement does not fall into it. "Customary address" is the usual term for it — the same institution as the President's address under Article 87.

**Statement 2 — correct, and this is where the disagreement lies.**
A State Legislature makes its own rules of procedure under Article 208. But the rule books the States actually made are modelled on the Lok Sabha's, and they carry a residuary provision: where these rules are silent on a matter, the rules and established practice of the Lok Sabha are followed, so far as they are applicable. In the gap, the Speaker's residuary power is exercised on Lok Sabha precedent rather than invented afresh. Statement 2 describes precisely this residuary situation — *"when a State Legislature does not have a rule on a particular matter"* — not a general subordination of State legislatures to Parliament.

**Why "1 only" is tempting but wrong.**
The solver almost certainly rejected statement 2 on the sound-sounding principle that each House is master of its own procedure and Parliament cannot dictate rules to a State Legislature. True — and irrelevant here. The statement makes no claim of compulsion; it says the State House *follows* the Lok Sabha rule in a gap, which is what its own rules direct it to do. Reading a constitutional command into "follows" is the error. Article 208(2) — pre-Constitution provincial rules continuing until new rules are made — is a different provision and is not a ground for calling statement 2 false.

**Takeaway:** on Article 176, check the quantifier ("first session of the year"). On procedure, distinguish *bound by* from *follows in the absence of its own rule*.
questions.tagging_note: Statement 2 (borrowing Lok Sabha rules of procedure) touches POL-18, but both statements are about State Legislature working, so POL-21 is primary.
questions.review_flag: Official key says c, worked solution said a (medium confidence).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. The United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) has a 'Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea and Air'.
2. The UNCAC is the ever-first legally binding global anti-corruption instrument.
3. A highlight of the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (UNTOC) is the inclusion of a specific chapter aimed at returning assets to their rightful owners from whom they had been taken illicitly.
4. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) is mandated by its member States to assist in the implementation of both UNCAC and UNTOC.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: 2 and 4 only.**

The question is one big swap between the two conventions:
- **(1) Wrong** — The **Smuggling of Migrants Protocol belongs to UNTOC (Palermo Convention)**, not UNCAC. UNTOC has three protocols: trafficking in persons, smuggling of migrants, firearms.
- **(2) Correct** — UNCAC (2003, in force 2005) is the **first legally binding global anti-corruption instrument**.
- **(3) Wrong** — The **asset-recovery chapter (Chapter V) is UNCAC's** landmark feature, not UNTOC's.
- **(4) Correct** — **UNODC is the guardian/secretariat for both** UNCAC and UNTOC.

India ratified UNCAC in 2011 and UNTOC in 2011.
questions.tagging_note: UNCAC/UNTOC/UNODC are UN conventions and a UN office — CAI-07 (global governance: treaties, conventions) is the closest fit, with CAI-04 for the UN system. No dedicated internal-security / transnational-crime topic exists in the vocabulary.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. As per recent amendment to the Indian Forest Act, 1927, forest dwellers have the right to fell the bamboos grown on forest areas.
2. As per the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, bamboo is a minor forest produce.
3. The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 allows ownership of minor forest produce to forest dwellers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: 2 and 3 only.**

- **(1) Wrong** — The **Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 removed bamboo from the definition of "tree" only where it grows in *non-forest* areas**. Bamboo standing on forest land is still a tree and felling/transit rules apply. The statement says "grown on forest areas" — that flips it.
- **(2) Correct** — FRA 2006 defines **minor forest produce** to include "bamboo, brushwood, stumps, cane, tussar, cocoons, honey, wax, lac, tendu/kendu leaves..." — bamboo is named first.
- **(3) Correct** — Section 3(1)(c) of FRA gives forest dwellers the **right of ownership, access to collect, use and dispose of** minor forest produce traditionally collected.

The 2017 amendment's purpose was to boost farmers' bamboo cultivation on private/non-forest land.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles ENV (Indian Forest Act 1927 amendment, FRA 2006, minor forest produce — ENV-09 lists FRA explicitly) and tribal rights under POL-23.
questions.transcription_note: Statement 1 sits at the foot of the left column on page 25; statements 2-3 and all options continue in the right column. Verified complete.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution of India safeguards one's right to marry the person of one's choice?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: Article 21.**

The right to marry a person of one's choice is read into the **right to life and personal liberty under Article 21** — it is part of personal autonomy, dignity and privacy.

Key cases: *Lata Singh v. State of UP* (2006), *Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M.* (2018, Hadiya case) — "the right to marry a person of one's choice is integral to Article 21"; *Shakti Vahini v. Union of India* (2018, khap panchayats) traced it to **Articles 19 and 21**, but the settled single-article answer is **21**.

(Art. 19 = freedoms of speech/movement/association; Art. 25 = freedom of religion; Art. 29 = minority cultural rights.)

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. According to the Indian Patents Act, a biological process to create a seed can be patented in India.
2. In India, there is no Intellectual Property Appellate Board.
3. Plant varieties are not eligible to be patented in India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: 3 only.**

- **(1) Wrong** — **Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970** bars patents on "plants and animals in whole or any part thereof other than micro-organisms, **including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes** for production or propagation of plants and animals." So a biological process to create a seed is **not** patentable.
- **(2) Wrong** — The **Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) existed** from 2003; it heard appeals from the Patent and Trade Marks registries. (It was abolished later, by the Tribunals Reforms Ordinance/Act of 2021 — irrelevant to a 2019 paper.)
- **(3) Correct** — Plant varieties are excluded from patenting; they get *sui generis* protection under the **Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001**, satisfying TRIPS Art. 27.3(b).
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects: IPR appears in both SNT-14 (S&T policy, institutions, IPR) and ECO-15 (industrial policy, IPR). Chose SNT-14 because the question tests patent-law institutions (IPAB) and patentability of biological processes / plant varieties (PPVFR Act), which sits closer to S&T-biotech than to industrial policy. No standalone IPR-law topic exists.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
The Environment Protection Act, 1986 empowers the Government of India to
1. state the requirement of public participation in the process of environmental protection, and the procedure and manner in which it is sought
2. lay down the standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (b) 2 only**

This is a text-matching question, not a spirit-of-the-law question. It asks what the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 **empowers the Government of India to do** — so each statement has to be located in the Act's own enumeration of powers.

**Statement 2 is correct — it is lifted almost verbatim from the Act.**
