Section 3(2)(iv) empowers the Central Government to take measures including "laying down standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources whatsoever." The same power reappears in the rule-making section, Section 6(2)(b), covering the maximum allowable limits of concentration of environmental pollutants for different areas. This is the legal basis for every emission norm notified under the Act. Statement 2 is beyond dispute.

**Statement 1 is wrong because it is not a power the Act confers.**
Section 3(2) lists fourteen heads of power: coordination of State action, a nationwide programme, ambient quality standards, emission standards, restriction of areas for industries, safeguards against accidents, handling of hazardous substances, examination of processes and materials, research, inspection, environmental laboratories, collection and dissemination of information, manuals and codes, and a residuary clause. Section 6 lists the matters on which rules may be made. **Neither list contains public participation, and the phrase "public participation" does not appear in the Act at all.** The closest the Act comes to the public is Section 19, which lets any person file a complaint in court after giving sixty days' notice to the Government — a citizen's route into *prosecution*, and a right of the citizen, not a power of the Government to prescribe when and how the public shall be consulted.

The requirement of public consultation in Indian environmental law lives one level down, in subordinate legislation: the public hearing introduced into the EIA regime in 1997 and now Chapter III of the **EIA Notification, 2006**, issued under Section 3 read with Rule 5 of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986. A notification is not the Act.

**Why (c) is the tempting wrong answer.**
The reasoning that leads to (c) is: the EIA public hearing is issued *under* the EPA, and clause (xiv) of Section 3(2) is a residuary power to take "such other measures as the Central Government deems necessary or expedient" — so the Act does in effect empower the Government to require public participation. That inference is legally arguable but it is not what the question asks. UPSC's convention in a two-statement "the Act empowers" question is to test the **enumerated text**: one statement is reproduced word-for-word from a clause, the other has no clause to sit in. If a residuary catch-all could validate any statement, statement 1 could never be false and the question would have no answer. The examiner has deliberately paired a verbatim clause with a plausible-sounding, procedurally specific power — "state the requirement of public participation… and the procedure and manner in which it is sought" — that is nowhere in the statute. A power written that precisely is the kind Parliament puts into a section when it means it; here Parliament did not.

Options (a) and (d) fail immediately, since statement 2 is textually certain.

**Revision card:** EPA 1986 Section 3(2) — fourteen heads, none of them public participation. Public participation in Indian environmental law = EIA Notification 2006 (public consultation), plus locus standi before the NGT. Do not import the notification's content back into the parent Act.
questions.review_flag: Official key says b, worked solution said c (medium confidence).

questions.stem: As per the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 in India, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Waste generator has to segregate waste into five categories.
The Rules are applicable to notified urban local bodies, notified towns and all industrial townships only.
The Rules provide for exact and elaborate criteria for the identification of sites for landfills and waste processing facilities.
It is mandatory on the part of waste generator that the waste generated in one district cannot be moved to another district.
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (c).**

**Schedule I of the SWM Rules, 2016 lays down detailed landfill siting criteria** — e.g. ≥100 m from a river, ≥200 m from a pond/highway/habitation/public park/water-supply well, ≥20 km from an airport/airbase (relaxable with AAI clearance), plus specifications for liners, leachate collection and closure.

Why the others fail:
- **(a)** Segregation is into **three** streams — biodegradable (wet), non-biodegradable (dry), and domestic hazardous — not five.
- **(b)** The 2016 Rules deliberately went **beyond municipal areas**: they also cover census towns, urban agglomerations, notified industrial townships, **railway stations, airports, ports, defence establishments, SEZs, places of pilgrimage and State/Central organisations**. The word "only" is fatal.
- **(d)** No such inter-district transport ban exists.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
As per the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018
1. if rules for fixed-term employment are implemented, it becomes easier for the firms/companies to lay off workers
2. no notice of termination of employment shall be necessary in the case of temporary workman
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: Both 1 and 2.**

The **2018 amendment extended "fixed term employment" to all sectors** (it had been allowed only in apparel manufacturing since 2016).

- **(1) Correct** — A fixed-term contract **lapses on its own by efflux of time**, so the employer owes **no notice and no retrenchment compensation** under the Industrial Disputes Act. Effectively it makes shedding workers easier — the exact reason trade unions opposed it. (The worker is entitled to the same wages, hours and statutory benefits as a permanent workman while employed, and pro-rata gratuity-type benefits.)
- **(2) Correct** — The **Model Standing Orders** provide that **no temporary workman (monthly-, weekly- or piece-rated), probationer or badli is entitled to notice or pay in lieu** if his services are terminated.

Both statements are consistent with the flexibility direction of the amendment, so (c).
questions.tagging_note: No topic in the vocabulary genuinely covers labour laws / labour reform (Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Rules, fixed-term employment, hire-and-fire, the Labour Codes). ECO-17 is used only because it is the nearest neighbour via unemployment and the labour market, and ECO-15 via industrial policy. This is a real gap: labour reform is a recurring Prelims theme with no home in the 186-topic tree.

questions.stem: The Service Area Approach was implemented under the purview of
options: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme
questions.explanation_md:
**The Service Area Approach (SAA), introduced by the RBI in April 1989, operates under the Lead Bank Scheme.**

- Lead Bank Scheme (1969, on Gadgil Study Group / Nariman Committee advice): one bank is made "lead" for each district and coordinates credit there.
- SAA extended that logic downwards — every rural/semi-urban **bank branch** was allotted a cluster of 15–25 villages as its "service area" for planning and lending. Branch credit plans → block plans → district credit plan.
- The village-allotment restriction was largely dispensed with in 2004 (except government-sponsored schemes), but SAA still sits inside the Lead Bank framework.

IRDP, MGNREGS and NSDM are employment/skilling programmes, not credit-planning frameworks.
questions.tagging_note: Service Area Approach (RBI, 1989) sits under the Lead Bank Scheme — rural credit planning / financial inclusion. No topic names the Lead Bank Scheme explicitly; ECO-06 (financial inclusion) is the closest, with ECO-04 (banking structure incl. RRBs, cooperatives) as the alternative home.

questions.stem:
With reference to the management of minor minerals in India, consider the following statements :
1. Sand is a 'minor mineral' according to the prevailing law in the country.
2. State Governments have the power to grant mining leases of minor minerals, but the powers regarding the formation of rules related to the grant of minor minerals lie with the Central Government.
3. State Governments have the power to frame rules to prevent illegal mining of minor minerals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Governing law: **Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957**.

**1. Correct.** Sec. 3(e) defines minor minerals as "building stones, gravel, **ordinary sand**, ordinary clay, boulder, limeshell, brick-earth..." — sand (other than sand used for prescribed industrial purposes) is a minor mineral.

**2. Incorrect — this is the deciding statement.** **Section 15 gives the *State* Government the power to make rules for grant of quarry/mining leases of minor minerals**, not the Centre. States both grant the leases and frame the rules; the Centre only issues non-binding guidelines (e.g. Sustainable Sand Mining Guidelines, 2016).

**3. Correct.** Sec. 23C empowers State Governments to frame rules to prevent illegal mining, transportation and storage of minerals.

So 1 and 3 only.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles GEO/ENV. Tests the MMDR Act's definition of minor minerals and the Centre/State rule-making split — a mining-law question. GEO-18 (India mineral resources) is the nearest topic; ENV-09 (environmental laws) covers the illegal-mining/regulatory angle. The vocabulary has no dedicated mineral-policy/MMDR topic.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Most of India's external debt is owed by governmental entities.
2. All of India's external debt is denominated in US dollars.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**1. Incorrect.** India's external debt is overwhelmingly **non-government**. Sovereign/government debt is only about a fifth of the total; the bulk is commercial borrowings (ECBs), NRI deposits and trade credit owed by private corporates and banks.

**2. Incorrect.** **The US dollar is dominant (~50%) but not exclusive** — India's external debt is also denominated in Indian rupee (the second largest share, chiefly FPI holdings of G-secs and rupee-denominated debt), SDR, Japanese yen and euro.

Both wrong → Neither 1 nor 2. Remember the shape: *mostly private, mostly but not only dollar*.

questions.stem: Which of the following is **not** included in the assets of a commercial bank in India?
options: Money at call and short notice
questions.explanation_md:
A bank's balance sheet: **what it owns = assets; what it owes = liabilities.**

**Deposits are money the bank owes to depositors — a liability, not an asset.** Along with capital, reserves and borrowings, deposits sit on the liabilities side.

Assets side of a commercial bank:
- Cash in hand and balances with RBI
- **Money at call and short notice** (very short-term lending to other banks)
- **Investments** (G-secs, SLR securities, etc.)
- **Advances** (loans given out)
- Fixed and other assets

A loan the bank *gives* is an asset; a deposit it *takes* is a liability.
questions.tagging_note: Tests the commercial-bank balance sheet (deposits are liabilities, not assets). No topic names bank balance sheets; ECO-04 (banking structure) is the closest, ECO-02 (money and banking) the alternative.

questions.stem:
In the context of India, which of the following factors is/are contributor/contributors to reducing the risk of a currency crisis?
1. The foreign currency earnings of India's IT sector
2. Increasing the government expenditure
3. Remittances from Indians abroad
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
A currency crisis risk falls when the country has a **steady inflow of foreign exchange** that is not debt-creating.

**1. Correct.** IT/software services exports are India's largest single source of net services earnings — a large, stable, non-debt forex inflow that cushions the current account.

**2. Incorrect — the deciding statement.** **Higher government expenditure widens the fiscal deficit, raises domestic demand and imports, and worsens the current account** — it *increases*, not reduces, currency pressure.

**3. Correct.** Remittances (India is the world's largest recipient) are a large, counter-cyclical, non-debt forex inflow; along with software exports they largely offset the merchandise trade deficit.

So 1 and 3 only.

questions.stem: Which one of the following suggested that the Governor should be an eminent person from outside the State and should be a detached figure without intense political links or should not have taken part in politics in the recent past?
options: National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2000)
questions.explanation_md:
**Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations (set up 1983, reported 1988).** Its recommendations on the Governor:

- Should be **eminent in some walk of life**
- Should be a **person from outside the State**
- Should be a **detached figure without intense political links**, and not too intimately connected with local politics of the State
- Should **not have taken too great a part in politics, particularly in the recent past**

The Punchhi Commission (2010) and the NCRWC (2000) later endorsed similar criteria, but **this exact four-point formulation is Sarkaria's**. The Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu) went much further — it wanted Article 356 and the Governor's discretionary powers deleted altogether.
questions.tagging_note: Sarkaria Commission recommendation on gubernatorial appointment — sits across POL-21 (Governor) and POL-15 (Centre–State relations, where the Sarkaria/Rajamannar commissions are studied).

questions.stem: Which of the following is issued by registered foreign portfolio investors to overseas investors who want to be part of the Indian stock market without registering themselves directly?
questions.explanation_md:
**Participatory Notes (P-Notes).**

- Offshore derivative instruments (ODIs) **issued by SEBI-registered Foreign Portfolio Investors to overseas investors** who want exposure to Indian shares without registering with SEBI themselves.
- The FPI buys the Indian security and issues a P-Note against it; returns flow to the P-Note holder.
- Concern: **anonymity of the end beneficiary** → round-tripping and money-laundering risk; SEBI has progressively tightened KYC, banned ODIs on derivatives for speculation, and levied issuance fees.

The others are money-market instruments: Certificate of Deposit (issued by banks), Commercial Paper (by corporates), Promissory Note (a debt acknowledgement under the NI Act).

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. As per law, the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority exists at both National and State levels.
2. People's participation is mandatory in the compensatory afforestation programmes carried out under the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016** (rules notified 2018) unlocked the ~₹50,000+ crore accumulated CAMPA corpus.

**1. Correct.** The Act creates a **National Compensatory Afforestation Fund (Public Account of India) and a State Fund in each State's Public Account**, and correspondingly a **National Authority and a State Authority** — CAMPA exists at both levels, statutorily. 90% of the money goes to States, 10% is retained nationally.

**2. Incorrect — the deciding statement.** **The Act contains no provision making people's participation (or Gram Sabha consent) mandatory.** This is precisely the criticism levelled at it — that afforestation is planted on land often already under community/forest-dwellers' use, with no requirement of consent under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.

So 1 only.

questions.stem:
In India, which of the following review the independent regulators in sectors like telecommunications, insurance, electricity, etc.?
1. Ad Hoc Committees set up by the Parliament
2. Parliamentary Department Related Standing Committees
3. Finance Commission
4. Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
5. NITI Aayog
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
Regulators like TRAI, IRDAI and CERC are creatures of statute and are **accountable to Parliament**.

**1. Correct.** Parliament can constitute **ad hoc committees** (select/joint committees, committees of inquiry) to examine a specific regulator or sector.

**2. Correct.** **Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs)** examine the working, budget demands and annual reports of ministries *and the bodies under them* — TRAI under the IT & Communications committee, IRDAI under Finance, CERC under Energy. **This is the routine, permanent review mechanism.**

**3. Incorrect.** The Finance Commission only recommends the sharing of tax revenue between Centre and States.

**4. Incorrect.** The FSLRC (2011–13, Justice Srikrishna) was a one-time body that reviewed *financial sector laws*; it is defunct and never covered telecom or electricity.

**5. Incorrect.** NITI Aayog is a think tank/advisory body — it has no oversight role over regulators.

So 1 and 2.
questions.tagging_note: Answer turns on Department-Related Standing Committees and ad hoc committees reviewing sectoral regulators — POL-19 (Parliamentary committees) is the core. The distractors (Finance Commission, FSLRC, NITI Aayog) pull in POL-24/POL-25; POL-25 included as the regulator/body angle. Sectoral regulators (TRAI, IRDAI, CERC) themselves have no dedicated topic.

questions.stem:
With reference to India's Five-Year Plans, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. From the Second Five-Year Plan, there was a determined thrust towards substitution of basic and capital good industries.
2. The Fourth Five-Year Plan adopted the objective of correcting the earlier trend of increased concentration of wealth and economic power.
3. In the Fifth Five-Year Plan, for the first time, the financial sector was included as an integral part of the Plan.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
**1. Correct.** The **Second Plan (1956–61, Mahalanobis model)** turned decisively to **import substitution in basic and capital goods industries** — heavy industry, steel plants (Bhilai, Rourkela, Durgapur), machine-building. Backed by the Industrial Policy Resolution, 1956.

**2. Correct.** The **Fourth Plan (1969–74)** — "growth with stability" and "progressive achievement of self-reliance" — explicitly sought to **correct the growing concentration of wealth and economic power**. Same period as bank nationalisation (1969) and the MRTP Act (1969).

**3. Incorrect — this is the deciding statement.** **It was the Eighth Plan (1992–97), the first plan of the liberalisation era, that brought the financial sector in as an integral part of the plan**, not the Fifth. The Fifth Plan (1974–79) was the *Garibi Hatao* / minimum-needs plan, terminated early in 1978.

So 1 and 2 only.

questions.stem:
With reference to Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), consider the following statements :
1. AIIB has more than 80 member nations.
2. India is the largest shareholder in AIIB.
3. AIIB does not have any members from outside Asia.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**AIIB is multilateral and global — its membership crossed 80+ and includes many non-Asian (regional and non-regional) members.**

- **1. Correct.** AIIB began with 57 founding members (2016) and expanded past 80 approved members by 2018-19 (100+ today). Headquarters: Beijing.
- **2. Wrong.** **China is the largest shareholder** (~26-30% voting share, effective veto on major decisions). **India is the second-largest shareholder** — and the largest borrower from AIIB.
- **3. Wrong.** AIIB has non-regional members — UK, Germany, France, Australia, Canada, Egypt, Brazil. The US and Japan are the notable absentees.

So only 1 → **(a)**.

*Trap:* India being the biggest *borrower* is confused with biggest *shareholder*.

questions.stem: What was the purpose of Inter-Creditor Agreement signed by Indian banks and financial institutions recently?
options: To lessen the Government of India's perennial burden of fiscal deficit and current account deficit
To support the infrastructure projects of Central and State Governments
To act as independent regulator in case of applications for loans of ₹ 50 crore or more
To aim at faster resolution of stressed assets of ₹ 50 crore or more which are under consortium lending
questions.explanation_md:
**The Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA, July 2018) came out of the Sunil Mehta Committee's "Project Sashakt" — a bank-led resolution framework for consortium NPAs.**

Key features:
- Applies to loan accounts of **₹50 crore and above under consortium / multiple banking**.
- The **lead bank** (largest exposure) prepares a resolution plan within 180 days.
- Approval needs **66% of lenders by value** — once approved, it binds all signatories.
- Dissenting lenders must either sell their exposure at a discount or buy out others.

It is an out-of-court, pre-IBC mechanism to speed up stressed-asset resolution — nothing to do with fiscal deficit, infrastructure funding, or regulation. → **(d)**

questions.stem: The Chairmen of public sector banks are selected by the
questions.explanation_md:
**Banks Board Bureau (BBB), operational from 1 April 2016, selects the whole-time directors and non-executive chairmen of PSBs and public-sector financial institutions/insurers.**

- Recommendation of the **P. J. Nayak Committee**; an interim body meant to evolve into a Bank Investment Company.
- It also advises PSBs on capital-raising, strategy and NPA management — but appointment is a **government (ACC) decision on BBB's recommendation**; the *selection* is BBB's job.
- RBI regulates, it does not select PSB chiefs. The Finance Ministry appoints on the recommendation; the bank's own management has no role.

→ **(a)**. (BBB was superseded by the **Financial Services Institutions Bureau, FSIB, in 2022** — post-dates the 2019 paper.)

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) is the first regulatory body set up by the Government of India.
2. One of the tasks of PNGRB is to ensure competitive markets for gas.
3. Appeals against the decisions of PNGRB go before the Appellate Tribunals for Electricity.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**PNGRB was set up under the PNGRB Act 2006 (functional 2007) — far from India's first regulator.**

- **1. Wrong.** Earlier regulators exist: **TRAI (1997), SEBI (1988/1992 statutory), CERC (1998), IRDA (1999)**. This is the deciding statement.
- **2. Correct.** PNGRB's stated mandate: protect consumer interests and **foster fair trade and competition** in downstream petroleum and gas — including authorising pipelines and city gas distribution networks.
- **3. Correct.** Appeals against PNGRB orders lie to the **Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL)**, which doubles as the appellate body for petroleum and gas.

Only 2 and 3 → **(b)**.
questions.tagging_note: Sectoral regulator (PNGRB) plus appellate route. No dedicated 'regulatory bodies' topic exists in the vocabulary; ECO-16 (services, infrastructure, energy) is the closest home, with GEO-18 (mineral and energy resources) as the sector link.

questions.stem:
With reference to communication technologies, what is/are the difference/differences between LTE (Long-Term Evolution) and VoLTE (Voice over Long-Term Evolution)?
1. LTE is commonly marketed as 3G and VoLTE is commonly marketed as advanced 3G.
2. LTE is data-only technology and VoLTE is voice-only technology.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are wrong — LTE is 4G, and VoLTE is voice carried *over* the same LTE data network, not a separate voice-only technology.**

- **1. Wrong.** LTE is marketed as **4G** (technically 3.9G / "4G LTE"); LTE-Advanced is the true IMT-Advanced 4G. Neither is 3G.
- **2. Wrong.** LTE is an all-IP **packet-switched data** network. Before VoLTE, phones fell back to 2G/3G circuit-switched networks for calls (**CSFB — Circuit Switched Fallback**). **VoLTE carries voice as IP packets over the LTE network itself**, so it is not "voice-only" — it rides on the data bearer, giving HD voice and simultaneous data use.

Neither → **(d)**.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017?
1. Pregnant women are entitled for three months pre-delivery and three months post-delivery paid leave.
2. Enterprises with crèches must allow the mother minimum six crèche visits daily.
3. Women with two children get reduced entitlements.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
**Answer: (c) 3 only**

The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 amended the 1961 Act. Test each statement against the actual numbers in the amended sections — every wrong statement here fails on a *number*, not on a concept.

**Statement 1 — incorrect (the split, not the total, is wrong).**
The amended Section 5(3) raises paid maternity leave from 12 to **26 weeks**. Twenty-six weeks is roughly six months, which is exactly what makes "three months + three months" look right. But the same sub-section fixes how those weeks may be distributed: **"not more than eight weeks shall precede the date of her expected delivery."** Eight weeks is under two months, not three. So a woman cannot take three months of the entitlement before delivery; the pre-delivery cap is 8 weeks, leaving at least 18 weeks after. The statement gets the total right by accident and the mandated split wrong — and the statement asserts the split, so it is false.

**Statement 2 — incorrect (four visits, not six).**
The new **Section 11A** requires every establishment with **50 or more employees** to provide a crèche facility, and says the employer **"shall allow four visits a day to the creche by the woman, which shall also include the interval for rest allowed to her."** The number in the statute is **four**, and those four are not four *extra* visits — the ordinary rest interval is counted inside them. The statement says "minimum six," which is simply not the figure in Section 11A. This is the single point on which the solver's answer turns, and it is a bare factual mismatch with the text.

**Statement 3 — correct (this is the entitlement tier the Act deliberately created).**
The 26-week entitlement is not universal. Section 5(3) as amended gives 26 weeks to a woman with **fewer than two surviving children**; a woman who **already has two or more surviving children** remains on **12 weeks**, of which not more than **6 weeks** may precede the expected date of delivery. So a woman with two children does receive a reduced entitlement — 12 weeks instead of 26, and a 6-week rather than 8-week pre-delivery window. The statement is a plain description of that two-tier structure.

Only statement 3 survives, so the answer is **(c)**.

**Why (b) "2 only" fails.**
Choosing (b) requires believing crèche visits are six and that the entitlement is uniform regardless of the number of surviving children. Both are wrong, and they fail independently:

- "Six visits" has no basis in Section 11A. The statute's number is four, and it is explicitly inclusive of the rest interval. There is no reading under which six is the statutory minimum.
- Treating statement 3 as false usually comes from reading "women with two children get reduced entitlements" as if the Act penalised mothers, and rejecting it as a discriminatory-sounding claim. But the Act really does condition the 26-week benefit on having fewer than two surviving children — the enhanced leave was targeted at the first two children, and the pre-existing 12-week benefit was left in place beyond that. The statement describes the law, not an opinion about it.

**The trap to remember.** All three statements are number traps built on plausible near-misses: 26 weeks ≈ six months (but capped at 8 weeks before delivery), crèche visits (four, not six), and the 26-week benefit (conditional on fewer than two surviving children, not universal). For this Act, memorise the four figures — **26 weeks / 8 weeks pre-delivery / 12 weeks for two-or-more surviving children / 50 employees for a crèche with 4 visits a day** — and the question answers itself.

Sources: [PRS India — text of the Act](https://prsindia.org/files/bills_acts/acts_parliament/2017/the-maternity-benefit-(amendment)-act,-2017.pdf), [S.S. Rana & Co. on Section 11A](https://ssrana.in/articles/creche-facility-maternity-benefit-amendment-act-2017/)

CAI-10 (schemes tracker) and ECO-17 (welfare schemes) are proxies, not genuine fits. A 'Social justice — labour laws, women, children, vulnerable sections' topic is missing from the syllabus tree and would carry a recurring band of GS1 questions.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is **not** a sub-index of the World Bank's 'Ease of Doing Business Index'?
questions.explanation_md:
**The World Bank's Ease of Doing Business Index measured regulatory procedures for a firm — never law and order or governance quality.**

The ten parameters were:
1. Starting a business
2. **Dealing with construction permits**
3. Getting electricity
4. **Registering property**
5. Getting credit
6. Protecting minority investors
7. **Paying taxes**
8. Trading across borders
9. Enforcing contracts
10. Resolving insolvency

**"Maintenance of law and order" is not among them** → **(a)**.

(Doing Business was discontinued in 2021 after data-irregularity findings; replaced by **B-READY**.)

questions.stem: In India, 'extended producer responsibility' was introduced as an important feature in which of the following?
options: The Bio-medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998
The Recycled Plastic (Manufacturing and Usage) Rules, 1999
The Food Safety and Standard Regulations, 2011
questions.explanation_md:
**Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) entered Indian law with the e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011** (notified 2011, effective 1 May 2012).

- EPR = the **producer's responsibility for a product extends to its end-of-life** — collection, channelisation and environmentally sound recycling, via take-back and collection centres.
- The 2011 e-waste rules were the **first Indian regulation to name EPR explicitly**; it was later carried into the **e-Waste Rules 2016** (with collection targets and PROs) and the **Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016/2022** and Battery Waste Rules 2022.
- The **Recycled Plastics Rules 1999** dealt with thickness and food-contact use of plastic carry bags, not EPR.

→ **(c)**

questions.stem: The economic cost of food grains to the Food Corporation of India is Minimum Support Price and bonus (if any) paid to the farmers plus
options: procurement incidentals and charges for godowns
questions.explanation_md:
**FCI's economic cost = MSP (+ bonus) + procurement incidentals + distribution cost.** Roughly three components:

1. **MSP / pooled cost of grain** — payment to the farmer.
2. **Procurement incidentals** — mandi tax, arhtiya commission, gunny bags, mandi labour, forwarding charges.
3. **Distribution cost** — freight, storage/godown charges, interest, handling, establishment and administrative overheads, transit and storage losses.

Options (a) and (b) are each only a fragment of the third head; (d) omits distribution/freight. The full third head is **distribution cost**, which subsumes godowns and interest → **(c)**.

*Scale check:* economic cost has run roughly **1.5x the MSP** for wheat and rice, which is why the food subsidy bill is large.

questions.stem: In the context of any country, which one of the following would be considered as part of its social capital?
options: The proportion of literates in the population
The stock of its buildings, other infrastructure and machines
The size of population in the working age group
The level of mutual trust and harmony in the society
questions.explanation_md:
**Social capital = the value embedded in relationships — trust, norms, reciprocity, networks, harmony.** (Putnam, Coleman, Bourdieu.)

Distinguish the four capitals:
- **(a) Literacy rate → human capital** (skills and knowledge embodied in people).
- **(b) Buildings, infrastructure, machines → physical capital.**
- **(c) Working-age population → human resource / demographic dividend**, not social capital.
- **(d) Mutual trust and harmony → social capital.** ✔

High social capital lowers transaction costs, improves collective action and institutional performance — which is why it is counted as "capital" at all.

→ **(d)**
questions.tagging_note: Definitional question on 'social capital' vs physical and human capital. No topic names capital typology explicitly; ECO-18 (human development) is the nearest genuine home, ECO-01 (basic concepts) the fallback.

questions.stem:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements :
1. No High Court shall have the jurisdiction to declare any central law to be constitutionally invalid.
2. An amendment to the Constitution of India cannot be called into question by the Supreme Court of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Both statements are wrong.**

**St. 1 — Wrong.** A High Court can absolutely strike down a central law. Judicial review is not a Supreme Court monopoly: Art. 226 (writs) plus Arts. 13, 245–246 let a High Court declare any law — Union or State — unconstitutional. Its ruling binds only within its territorial jurisdiction; that is a limit on *reach*, not on *jurisdiction to declare*.

**St. 2 — Wrong.** A constitutional amendment **can** be challenged. Art. 368 amendments escape Art. 13's definition of "law" (Art. 13(4), added by the 24th Amendment), but **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** established that an amendment damaging the **basic structure** is void. Applied repeatedly — Minerva Mills, Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, the NJAC/99th Amendment struck down in 2015.

Hence **(d) Neither 1 nor 2**.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
1. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) exchange rates are calculated by comparing the prices of the same basket of goods and services in different countries.
2. In terms of PPP dollars, India is the sixth largest economy in the world.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**St. 1 — Correct.** PPP exchange rate is exactly that: the rate at which an **identical basket of goods and services** costs the same in two countries. It strips out price-level differences, which is why PPP GDP > nominal GDP for low-cost economies like India.

**St. 2 — Wrong.** **In PPP terms India was the *third* largest economy** (behind China and the USA) — it has held that spot since about 2014, worth roughly $10–11 trillion PPP in 2019. "Sixth largest" is India's rank in **nominal** GDP terms (5th–7th, jostling with the UK and France).

The trap is swapping the two rankings. Remember the pair: **nominal ≈ 5th/6th, PPP = 3rd**.

Hence **(a) 1 only**.
questions.tagging_note: PPP exchange rates sit between ECO-12 (external sector, exchange rate) and ECO-01 (GDP/national income comparison). Statement 1 is the exchange-rate mechanics (ECO-12); statement 2 is a size-of-economy fact usually parked under ECO-01. Primary set to ECO-12 because the concept being tested is the exchange-rate construct itself.

questions.stem:
With reference to the cultivation of Kharif crops in India in the last five years, consider the following statements :
1. Area under rice cultivation is the highest.
2. Area under the cultivation of jowar is more than that of oilseeds.
3. Area of cotton cultivation is more than that of sugarcane.
4. Area under sugarcane cultivation has steadily decreased.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**St. 1 — Correct.** Rice occupies about **43–44 million ha**, the largest area of any crop in India, kharif or otherwise.

**St. 2 — Wrong.** Jowar is down to roughly **5 million ha** and shrinking; **total oilseeds cover about 26 million ha** (groundnut, soyabean, rapeseed-mustard etc.). Oilseeds are far larger.

**St. 3 — Correct.** **Cotton ≈ 12–13 million ha vs sugarcane ≈ 5 million ha.** Cotton is comfortably bigger.

**St. 4 — Wrong.** Sugarcane area has *fluctuated* with the cane-price/arrears cycle (roughly 4.4–5.1 million ha), and actually rose in 2017–19. Nothing "steady" about it — and words like *steadily decreased* are almost always the giveaway in area/production statements.

Only 1 and 3 stand — **(a)**.

questions.stem: Among the agricultural commodities imported by India, which one of the following accounts for the highest imports in terms of value in the last five years?
questions.explanation_md:
**Vegetable (edible) oils** — India's single largest agricultural import by value, around **₹70,000–75,000 crore (~$10 billion) a year**, roughly **60% of domestic edible-oil consumption** imported.

Composition: **palm oil** from Indonesia and Malaysia (the bulk), **soyabean oil** from Argentina/Brazil, **sunflower oil** from Ukraine/Russia.

Pulses were the number two item and spiked to about $4 billion in 2016–17, but collapsed after 2017 once import duties and quantitative restrictions were imposed and domestic output recovered. Spices and fresh fruits are an order of magnitude smaller — India is a **net exporter** of spices.

Hence **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles agriculture economy and external trade: the fact tested is India's edible-oil import dependence. ECO-14 (agriculture) is the closest anchor; ECO-12 (BoP/trade) and GEO-17 (crops) are genuine secondaries. No topic in the tree is specifically 'India's agricultural trade composition'.

questions.stem: In the context of polity, which one of the following would you accept as the most appropriate definition of liberty?
options: Protection against the tyranny of political rulers
Opportunity to do whatever one likes
questions.explanation_md:
The question asks for the **most appropriate** definition, so it wants the modern **positive** conception, not the older negative one.

- (a) Protection against tyranny of rulers — too narrow; that is one *safeguard* of liberty, not liberty itself.
- (b) Absence of restraint — the classic **negative** definition, and an incomplete one: liberty needs *some* restraints to exist at all.
- (c) Doing whatever one likes — that is **licence**, not liberty. "Liberty for the pike is death for the minnows" (R.H. Tawney).
- (d) **Opportunity to develop oneself fully — correct.** This is **Laski's** formulation: liberty is the maintenance of an atmosphere in which people have the opportunity to be their best selves. It is the positive, enabling view that fits the Indian constitutional scheme — the Preamble's "liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship" read with the Directive Principles.

Hence **(d)**.
questions.tagging_note: GAP: no topic in the vocabulary covers political theory / conceptual definitions (liberty, equality, justice as ideas). This is a Polity-theory conceptual question, not a constitutional-provision question. POL-04 (Preamble) is the nearest anchor because liberty is a Preamble value, and POL-08 (Right to Freedom) touches it, but neither genuinely teaches the positive-vs-negative liberty distinction the question turns on. Consider a 'political theory / key concepts' topic if this recurs.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is **not** the most likely measure the Government/RBI takes to stop the slide of Indian rupee?
options: Curbing imports of non-essential goods and promoting exports
Encouraging Indian borrowers to issue rupee denominated Masala Bonds
Easing conditions relating to external commercial borrowing
questions.explanation_md:
A falling rupee is fixed by **pulling dollars in and pushing dollar demand down**. Check each:

- (a) **Curb non-essential imports, push exports** → cuts the trade deficit, reduces dollar demand. A real measure (done in Sept 2018).
- (b) **Masala Bonds** → rupee-denominated bonds sold abroad; the **exchange-rate risk sits with the foreign investor**, and the inflow is in foreign currency. Supports the rupee. A real measure.
- (c) **Easing ECB norms** → lets Indian firms borrow more abroad, bringing dollars in. A real measure (ECB rules were relaxed in 2018).
- (d) **Expansionary monetary policy — this is the odd one out.** Cutting rates and expanding money supply **narrows the interest-rate differential, triggers capital outflows and raises inflation — all of which weaken the rupee further.** To defend the currency a central bank *tightens*, it does not ease.

Hence **(d)**.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
The Reserve Bank of India's recent directives relating to 'Storage of Payment System Data', popularly known as data diktat, command the payment system providers that
1. they shall ensure that entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India
2. they shall ensure that the systems are owned and operated by public sector enterprises
3. they shall submit the consolidated system audit report to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India by the end of the calendar year
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
RBI circular of **6 April 2018 on Storage of Payment System Data** (compliance by 15 Oct 2018).

**St. 1 — Correct.** The **entire data relating to payment systems** — end-to-end transaction details, plus information collected, carried or processed as part of the message or payment instruction — **must be stored in a system only in India**. This is the core "data localisation" mandate.

**St. 2 — Wrong.** **No public-sector ownership requirement anywhere in the circular.** It applies to *all* payment system providers — Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, WhatsApp Pay included. RBI regulates them; it does not nationalise them.

**St. 3 — Wrong.** The **System Audit Report had to go to the RBI**, not the CAG, and had to be audited by a **CERT-In empanelled auditor** — deadline **31 December 2018**. The CAG audits government accounts, not private payment firms.

Hence **(a) 1 only**.
questions.tagging_note: RBI's payment-data localisation directive straddles ECO-20 (payments/new economy), ECO-03 (RBI as regulator) and SNT-10 (data protection/localisation). Primary set to ECO-20 as payment systems are its explicit scope; statement 3 also touches POL-24 (CAG) but only as a distractor, so it is not tagged.

questions.stem: Which of the following adopted a law on data protection and privacy for its citizens known as 'General Data Protection Regulation' in April 2016 and started implementation of it from 25th May, 2018?
questions.explanation_md:
**The European Union.** GDPR (Regulation 2016/679) was **adopted 27 April 2016** with a two-year transition, and became **enforceable on 25 May 2018** — the dates in the stem match exactly.

Key features worth carrying into an answer: applies **extraterritorially** to anyone processing EU residents' data, gives the **right to be forgotten**, data portability and explicit consent, and carries fines of up to **4% of global annual turnover or €20 million**, whichever is higher. It replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive.

The USA has no single federal privacy law (only sectoral ones plus California's CCPA); Canada has PIPEDA; Australia has the Privacy Act 1988.

Hence **(c)**.
questions.tagging_note: GDPR is a data-protection law (SNT-10) but reaches the exam as an international-affairs/current-affairs fact about the EU (CAI-07). Primary set to SNT-10 since the subject matter is data protection and privacy.

questions.stem: Recently, India signed a deal known as 'Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field' with which of the following countries?
questions.explanation_md:
**Russia.** The **"Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field"** was signed at the **19th India–Russia Annual Summit, New Delhi, October 2018** (the Modi–Putin summit that also produced the S-400 deal).

It covers **Kudankulam units 5 and 6**, a possible **second Russian-built nuclear site in India**, and — the distinctive bit — **joint civil-nuclear work in third countries, notably the Rooppur plant in Bangladesh**, plus cooperation in nuclear science, small modular reactors and non-power applications.

Don't confuse it with the **Japan** civil nuclear agreement (2016), the **US** 123 Agreement (2008), or the UK, which has no such India nuclear pact.

Hence **(b)**.

questions.stem: The money multiplier in an economy increases with which one of the following?
options: Increase in the cash reserve ratio
Increase in the banking habit of the population
Increase in the statutory liquidity ratio
Increase in the population of the country
questions.explanation_md:
Money multiplier **m = (1 + c) / (c + r)**, where **c** = currency-to-deposit ratio held by the public and **r** = reserve ratio of banks. The multiplier **rises when c or r falls**.

- (a) **Higher CRR** → banks must park more with RBI, less to lend → multiplier **falls**. Wrong.
- (b) **Better banking habit — correct.** More of the public's money sits in **deposits** rather than as cash in hand, so **c falls** and each rupee of high-powered money supports more credit creation → multiplier **rises**.
- (c) **Higher SLR** → more funds locked in government securities, less lendable → multiplier **falls**. Wrong.
- (d) **Population growth** → affects money *demand*, not the deposit-creation ratio. No direct link. Wrong.

Hence **(b)**.

questions.stem:
In the context of digital technologies for entertainment, consider the following statements :
1. In Augmented Reality (AR), a simulated environment is created and the physical world is completely shut out.
2. In Virtual Reality (VR), images generated from a computer are projected onto real-life objects or surroundings.
3. AR allows individuals to be present in the world and improves the experience using the camera of smart-phone or PC.
4. VR closes the world, and transposes an individual, providing complete immersion experience.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
The question deliberately **swaps the AR and VR definitions in statements 1 and 2**.

- **1 — Wrong.** "Simulated environment, physical world completely shut out" is **VR**, not AR.
- **2 — Wrong.** "Computer-generated images projected onto real-life objects/surroundings" is **AR**, not VR.
- **3 — Correct.** AR keeps you in the real world and overlays information through a phone/PC camera (Pokémon Go, Google Lens).
- **4 — Correct.** VR closes off the real world and transposes the user into a fully immersive digital environment (headsets like Oculus/HTC Vive).

So **3 and 4 only** → option (b).

*Memory hook:* **A**R **A**dds to reality; **V**R **V**anishes it.
questions.tagging_note: AR/VR is not named anywhere in the vocabulary — a genuine gap. SNT-09 (IT and computing — AI/ML, quantum, blockchain, cloud, 5G/6G) is the nearest home for consumer digital tech; SNT-13 (sensors, everyday tech) is a weaker second. Consider adding immersive tech to SNT-09's scope note.

questions.stem: The word 'Denisovan' is sometimes mentioned in media in reference to
options: fossils of a kind of dinosaurs
a cave system found in North-East India
a geological period in the history of Indian subcontinent
questions.explanation_md:
**Denisovans are an extinct archaic human species/subspecies**, known mainly from finger-bone and tooth fragments found in **Denisova Cave, Altai Mountains, Siberia (Russia)** in 2008–2010, identified through ancient DNA.

Key points:
- Contemporaries and cousins of Neanderthals; both share a common ancestor with modern humans.
- Modern **Melanesians, Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry ~3–5% Denisovan DNA**; the EPAS1 "high-altitude" gene in Tibetans is a Denisovan legacy.
- A jawbone from **Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe (Tibetan Plateau)** was later confirmed Denisovan.

Not a dinosaur, not a North-East Indian cave, not a geological period.
questions.tagging_note: Real vocabulary gap: human evolution / hominin species (Denisovans, Neanderthals, Homo naledi) has no topic. ANM-01 'Prehistory and the Indus Valley Civilisation' is the only place prehistory appears, but it is a history topic and this is palaeoanthropology, usually asked as a science-and-tech current-affairs item. SNT-01 covers cell/genetics/human systems, not evolution, so it does not fit either. Straddles ANM and SNT.

questions.stem: With reference to the recent developments in science, which one of the following statements is **not** correct?
options: Functional chromosomes can be created by joining segments of DNA taken from cells of different species.
Pieces of artificial functional DNA can be created in laboratories.
A piece of DNA taken out from an animal cell can be made to replicate outside a living cell in a laboratory.
Cells taken out from plants and animals can be made to undergo cell division in laboratory petri dishes.
questions.explanation_md:
The question asks which is **NOT** correct.

- **(b) Correct.** Craig Venter's team chemically synthesised a functional bacterial genome (*Mycoplasma mycoides* JCVI-syn1.0, 2010) — artificial functional DNA is routinely made in labs.
- **(c) Correct.** **PCR** replicates DNA outside a living cell, in a tube. Basic biotech.
- **(d) Correct.** Plant and animal **tissue culture** in petri dishes is standard practice.
- **(a) Is the odd one out.** Joining random DNA segments from different species does not by itself give a *functional chromosome* — a chromosome needs a working **centromere, telomeres and origins of replication compatible with the host cell**, and species-specific regulation. Recombinant DNA and hybrid vectors exist, but a **cross-species patchwork does not spontaneously behave as a functional chromosome**.

So (a) is the statement that is not correct.

*Note:* This is one of the more debated 2019 questions — some sources argue artificial/yeast chromosome work makes (a) defensible. Judge it by elimination: (b), (c), (d) are unarguably true.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
A digital signature is
1. an electronic record that identifies the certifying authority issuing it
2. used to serve as a proof of identity of an individual to access information or server on Internet
3. an electronic method of signing an electronic document and ensuring that the original content is unchanged
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
**Official answer: (c) — 3 only.**

The whole question turns on one compound term being split apart: **"digital signature"** versus **"Digital Signature Certificate" (DSC)**. Statements 1 and 2 describe the *certificate*; only statement 3 describes the *signature*.

**Statement 3 — correct.** This is the definition itself. Under Section 2(1)(p) read with Section 3 of the IT Act, 2000, a digital signature is the authentication of an electronic record by an electronic method: the document is passed through a hash function and the hash is encrypted with the signer's private key. Two things follow, and statement 3 names exactly those two — it is a *method of signing an electronic document*, and *any alteration to the content* changes the hash, so tampering is detectable. Signing plus integrity. Nothing more is claimed.

**Statement 1 — wrong, it defines the DSC.** "An electronic record that identifies the certifying authority issuing it" is lifted from the description of a Digital Signature *Certificate* (Sections 35–36, IT Act). A DSC is a file issued by a licensed Certifying Authority under the Controller of Certifying Authorities; it names the CA, the subscriber, the public key and the validity period. The digital signature is not a record that names a CA — it is a block of ciphertext computed from the document and the private key. It carries no CA's name inside it. The certificate identifies the CA; the signature does not.

**Statement 2 — wrong, it defines a digital ID / certificate-based login.** "Proof of identity of an individual to access information or server on Internet" is the function of a digital ID — again the certificate, or an SSL/TLS certificate on the server side. A raw digital signature proves only that whoever holds a particular private key signed a particular document. It proves *nothing about who that person is*. The binding of "this public key belongs to this named individual" is done entirely by the CA-issued certificate. Strip the certificate away and the signature is anonymous mathematics. Identity is the certificate's job, authorship-and-integrity is the signature's job — and this statement asks for identity.

**Why (d) is tempting and fails.** In everyday use the DSC and the signature travel together — you buy a "digital signature" from eMudhra and what arrives is a certificate on a USB token, so all three statements feel like descriptions of the same purchase. Statement 2 is the sharper trap, because certificate-based authentication really does involve a signing operation under the hood, so a technically strong candidate can talk themselves into it. But UPSC is testing the legal definitions of the IT Act, where "digital signature" and "Digital Signature Certificate" are two separately defined things with separate sections. Marking (d) means accepting that the signature *is* the certificate, and the Act says it is not.

**Rule to carry forward:** when a statement about a digital signature mentions a certifying authority, a validity period, or proving *who you are*, it has quietly slid to the certificate. The signature itself only ever does two things — asserts that this key signed this document, and reveals if the document changed afterwards.
questions.tagging_note: Digital signatures sit at the boundary of SNT-10 (cybersecurity, data protection — PKI and certifying authorities) and POL-27 (e-governance, IT Act machinery). Tagged as SNT because the question tests what a digital signature technically is, not the statutory framework.
questions.review_flag: Official key says c, worked solution said d (high confidence).

questions.stem:
In the context of wearable technology, which of the following tasks is/are accomplished by wearable devices?
1. Location identification of a person
2. Sleep monitoring of a person
3. Assisting the hearing impaired person
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
All three are routine wearable functions.

- **1 — Yes.** GPS-enabled smartwatches and fitness bands track location; used in running apps and child/elderly trackers.
- **2 — Yes.** Fitbit/Mi Band-class devices monitor sleep stages using accelerometers and heart-rate sensors.
- **3 — Yes.** **Hearing aids and cochlear-implant processors are wearable devices**; smart hearables also do live captioning and sound amplification.

**1, 2 and 3 → option (d).**

General UPSC heuristic: for "what can technology do" questions, technology is usually more capable than the option-setter's trap implies. Do not artificially restrict the definition of "wearable".
questions.tagging_note: Wearable technology has no dedicated topic. SNT-13 (everyday physics and chemistry; robotics, drones and sensors) is the closest fit via sensors; SNT-09 covers the computing/connectivity side.

questions.stem:
'RNA interference (RNAi)' technology has gained popularity in the last few years. Why?
1. It is used in developing gene silencing therapies.
2. It can be used in developing therapies for the treatment of cancer.
3. It can be used to develop hormone replacement therapies.
4. It can be used to produce crop plants that are resistant to viral pathogens.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
RNAi uses small RNA molecules (siRNA/miRNA) to **silence a specific gene at the mRNA level**, degrading the transcript before translation.

- **1 — Correct.** Gene silencing therapy is the very definition of RNAi; **Patisiran (2018) was the first FDA-approved siRNA drug**, for hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis.
- **2 — Correct.** Cancer therapy research uses RNAi to switch off oncogenes and drug-resistance genes.
- **3 — Wrong.** **Hormone replacement therapy supplies a missing hormone; RNAi only switches genes off, it cannot add a product.** This is the deciding statement.
- **4 — Correct.** RNAi gives virus-resistant crops — e.g. **papaya ringspot virus-resistant papaya**, virus-resistant beans, and *Bt*-adjacent RNAi traits against pests.

**1, 2 and 4 → option (a).**

Option (d) says "1 and 4 only", which wrongly drops the well-established cancer application.

questions.stem: Recently, scientists observed the merger of giant 'blackholes' billions of light-years away from the Earth. What is the significance of this observation?
options: Possibility of inter-galactic space travel through 'wormhole' was confirmed.
It enabled the scientists to understand 'singularity'.
questions.explanation_md:
**Merging black holes are detected through the gravitational waves they emit** — ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein's General Theory of Relativity (1916).

- First direct detection: **LIGO, 14 September 2015 (announced Feb 2016)** — merger of two black holes ~1.3 billion light-years away.
- **2017 Nobel Prize in Physics**: Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish, Kip Thorne.
- India's contribution: **LIGO-India**, approved for Hingoli, Maharashtra.

Why the others fail: the **Higgs boson** was detected at the **LHC/CERN (2012)** — a particle collider result, not astronomy. Wormhole travel remains unconfirmed speculation. Singularities cannot be observed; they lie inside the event horizon.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are the reasons for the occurrence of multi-drug resistance in microbial pathogens in India?
1. Genetic predisposition of some people
2. Taking incorrect doses of antibiotics to cure diseases
3. Using antibiotics in livestock farming
4. Multiple chronic diseases in some people
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
Antimicrobial resistance arises from **selection pressure on the microbe**, not from human genetics.

- **1 — Wrong.** "Genetic predisposition of some people" is irrelevant — **resistance is a property of the bacterium's genome, not the patient's.**
- **2 — Correct.** Incomplete/incorrect antibiotic courses leave partially susceptible bacteria alive to multiply — the classic driver, especially in TB (MDR-TB, XDR-TB).
- **3 — Correct.** Antibiotics as growth promoters and prophylactics in poultry, dairy and aquaculture push resistance into the food chain. **Colistin use in poultry** was a major Indian concern; India banned colistin as a feed additive in 2019.
- **4 — Wrong.** Having multiple chronic diseases raises a person's *risk of infection*, but does not itself create resistance in the pathogen.

**2 and 3 only → option (b).**

questions.stem: What is Cas9 protein that is often mentioned in news?
options: A molecular scissors used in targeted gene editing
A biosensor used in the accurate detection of pathogens in patients
A gene that makes plants pest-resistant
A herbicidal substance synthesized in genetically modified crops
questions.explanation_md:
**Cas9 (CRISPR-associated protein 9) is a bacterial endonuclease — a "molecular scissors" that cuts DNA at a site specified by a guide RNA.**

How it works: the **guide RNA** finds the matching 20-base DNA sequence (next to a PAM site) and Cas9 makes a double-strand break; the cell's repair machinery then disrupts or replaces the gene.

- Origin: a bacterial adaptive immune system against bacteriophages.
- **2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry**: Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna.
- Not a biosensor, not a plant pest-resistance gene (that is *Bt cry* genes), not a herbicide (that is glyphosate, with the *EPSPS/Roundup Ready* trait).

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is **not** correct?
options: Hepatitis B virus is transmitted much like HIV.
Hepatitis B, unlike Hepatitis C, does not have a vaccine.
Globally, the number of people infected with Hepatitis B and C viruses are several times more than those infected with HIV.
Some of those infected with Hepatitis B and C viruses do not show the symptoms for many years.
questions.explanation_md:
The question asks which is **NOT** correct.

- **(b) is false — and it is exactly backwards. Hepatitis B HAS a safe, effective vaccine (part of India's Universal Immunisation Programme, given in the pentavalent vaccine and at birth); it is Hepatitis C that has NO vaccine.** Hep C is instead curable with direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir etc.).
- **(a) Correct.** HBV spreads by blood, unsafe injections, sexual contact and mother-to-child — the same routes as HIV, and HBV is far more infectious per exposure.
- **(c) Correct.** Roughly **296 million with chronic HBV and ~58 million with HCV worldwide, against ~38 million with HIV** — several times more.
- **(d) Correct.** Both are notorious for remaining asymptomatic for years, surfacing only as cirrhosis or liver cancer — hence the "silent epidemic" label.

Answer: **(b)**.
